She has been trying to conceive for 18 months without success. Previous transvaginal ultrasound showed a 4 cm left ovarian endometrioma. She has tried combined oral contraceptive pill and oral progestogens, which provided partial symptom relief but she ceased them to attempt pregnancy. On examination, there is a fixed retroverted uterus with tender nodularity in the uterosacral ligaments and rectovaginal septum.

data_table.Investigations: AMH 18 pmol/L (age-appropriate), CA-125 82 U/mL (ref < 35), day 3 FSH 7.2 IU/L, partner semen analysis normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management approach?

options.text: Resume combined oral contraceptive pill continuously for 6 months to suppress disease before natural conception attempts
options.rationale: While hormonal suppression improves symptoms, there is no evidence that a period of hormonal suppression prior to attempting conception improves subsequent fertility. This patient has been trying to conceive for 18 months and hormonal treatment further delays fertility investigation and treatment. (Source: RANZCOG - Endometriosis)

options.text: Referral to a multidisciplinary endometriosis centre for laparoscopic excision with concurrent fertility planning
options.rationale: This patient has deep infiltrating endometriosis (DIE) with evidence of rectovaginal and uterosacral involvement, an ovarian endometrioma, cyclical bowel symptoms suggesting bowel wall involvement, and 18 months of unexplained infertility. Management requires referral to a multidisciplinary endometriosis centre with advanced laparoscopic skills and colorectal surgical support. Surgical excision of DIE and cystectomy of the endometrioma can improve pain symptoms and natural conception rates. Concurrent fertility planning with reproductive medicine input is appropriate given her subfertility. (Source: RANZCOG - Endometriosis)

options.text: Commence GnRH agonist (leuprorelin) with add-back HRT for 6 months followed by IVF with no surgical intervention
options.rationale: GnRH agonist therapy suppresses endometriosis but does not improve fertility and further delays conception. A 4 cm endometrioma may also impair oocyte retrieval and ovarian response during IVF. Surgical treatment of the endometrioma before IVF is generally recommended when endometriomas are 4 cm or above. (Source: ESHRE - Endometriosis Guideline)

options.text: Proceed directly to IVF without surgical treatment to minimise further delay in achieving fertility this year
options.rationale: While IVF may ultimately be needed, proceeding directly without addressing the 4 cm endometrioma and deep infiltrating disease is suboptimal. Endometriomas 4 cm or larger can impair oocyte retrieval, and surgical excision of moderate-severe endometriosis has been shown to improve natural conception rates. A planned surgical approach with concurrent fertility planning optimises outcomes. (Source: RANZCOG - Endometriosis)

options.text: Trial of dienogest 2 mg daily for 3 months as targeted endometriosis treatment while continuing to attempt conception
options.rationale: Dienogest is an effective progestogen for endometriosis symptom control but is an oral progestogen that inhibits ovulation and is used as a contraceptive. Concurrent use while trying to conceive is contradictory. Hormonal treatments for endometriosis are not compatible with active fertility attempts. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Gynaecology)

explanation.summary: Deep infiltrating endometriosis is defined as endometriotic lesions penetrating more than 5 mm below the peritoneal surface, commonly involving the uterosacral ligaments, rectovaginal septum, and bowel wall. The combination of dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, cyclical dyschezia with rectal bleeding, and a fixed retroverted uterus with rectovaginal nodularity is highly suggestive of DIE with bowel involvement. Management should occur at a multidisciplinary endometriosis centre with advanced laparoscopic and colorectal surgical expertise. Surgical excision improves both pain and fertility outcomes. AMH should be measured before endometrioma surgery as cystectomy can reduce ovarian reserve.
key_points: Cyclical dyschezia with rectal bleeding strongly suggests bowel endometriosis
DIE requires surgical management at a multidisciplinary centre with colorectal surgical support
Surgical excision of moderate-severe endometriosis improves natural conception rates
AMH measurement before endometrioma cystectomy helps counsel about ovarian reserve risk
explanation.pearls: Endometrioma cystectomy (stripping technique) removes 1-6 mL of normal ovarian cortex with each procedure, potentially reducing AMH by 30-40% - bilateral cystectomy should only be performed by experienced surgeons with ovarian reserve implications discussed preoperatively.

stem: A 27-year-old woman at 14 weeks gestation following IVF presents with sudden onset right iliac fossa pain radiating to the right flank, accompanied by nausea and vomiting. She describes the pain as intermittent and colicky, having started 4 hours ago. She has a known 8 cm right ovarian cyst that was identified at her IVF egg collection and has been monitored. On examination, there is tenderness in the right iliac fossa with guarding.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 98 bpm, BP 115/72 mmHg, Temp 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: WCC 12.8 x10^9/L, CRP 18 mg/L, urinalysis negative, fetal heart rate on Doppler 158 bpm. Ultrasound: enlarged right ovary 9 cm with peripherally displaced follicles and absent intraovarian venous flow on Doppler, free fluid in pouch of Douglas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Conservative management with analgesia and antiemetics, observation for 24 hours, and repeat ultrasound tomorrow
options.rationale: Ovarian torsion is a surgical emergency. Delayed surgery risks ovarian necrosis, peritonitis, and sepsis. The combination of sudden-onset colicky pain, enlarged ovary with absent venous flow on Doppler, and clinical features is highly suggestive of torsion. Conservative management is inappropriate when torsion is suspected. (Source: RANZCOG - Ovarian Masses in Pregnancy)

options.text: Arrange urgent appendicectomy as the most likely diagnosis is acute appendicitis given the right iliac fossa pain
options.rationale: While appendicitis is an important differential for right iliac fossa pain in pregnancy, the ultrasound findings of an enlarged ovary with absent venous flow and a known ovarian cyst make ovarian torsion the most likely diagnosis. The upward displacement of the appendix during pregnancy also makes the location atypical for appendicitis at 14 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG - Ovarian Masses in Pregnancy)

options.text: Urgent laparoscopic detorsion with ovarian conservation, performed by a surgeon experienced in laparoscopy during pregnancy
options.rationale: Ovarian torsion in pregnancy requires urgent surgical intervention. Laparoscopic detorsion with ovarian conservation is the standard approach regardless of the macroscopic appearance of the ovary, as ovarian recovery rates after detorsion exceed 90% even when the ovary appears dusky or black. Laparoscopy is safe in the first and second trimesters and is preferred over laparotomy. The cyst may be drained or excised if necessary, but the ovary should be preserved. (Source: RANZCOG - Ovarian Masses in Pregnancy)

options.text: Urgent laparotomy with right oophorectomy given the absent Doppler flow indicating likely complete ovarian necrosis
options.rationale: Oophorectomy should be avoided as the ovary has high recovery potential even when Doppler flow is absent and the ovary appears macroscopically compromised. Studies show ovarian viability rates above 90% after detorsion. Laparotomy is also unnecessarily invasive when laparoscopy is feasible. Ovarian preservation is especially important in this young woman who conceived through IVF. (Source: RANZCOG - Ovarian Masses in Pregnancy)

options.text: MRI pelvis to confirm the diagnosis before proceeding to surgery, with analgesia and antiemetics in the interim
options.rationale: When the clinical presentation and ultrasound findings are consistent with ovarian torsion, MRI should not delay surgical intervention. MRI has reasonable sensitivity for torsion but is not required when ultrasound shows absent venous flow in a symptomatic patient with a known risk factor. Time to surgery directly correlates with ovarian salvage rates. (Source: RANZCOG - Ovarian Masses in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Ovarian torsion in pregnancy most commonly occurs in the first trimester and early second trimester, particularly in the context of ovarian hyperstimulation from IVF or large ovarian cysts. The classic presentation is sudden-onset colicky pelvic pain with nausea and vomiting. Ultrasound findings of an enlarged ovary with absent or reduced venous flow on Doppler support the diagnosis. Urgent laparoscopic detorsion with ovarian conservation is the treatment of choice - oophorectomy is almost never necessary and the ovary has remarkable recovery potential. In early pregnancy, loss of the corpus luteum-bearing ovary before 10-12 weeks may precipitate miscarriage unless exogenous progesterone is supplemented.
key_points: IVF-stimulated ovaries and large cysts are major risk factors for torsion in pregnancy
Absent venous flow on Doppler in a symptomatic patient is highly suggestive of torsion
Laparoscopic detorsion with ovarian conservation is standard regardless of ovarian appearance
Ovarian recovery rates after detorsion exceed 90% even when the ovary appears necrotic
explanation.pearls: The whirlpool sign on transvaginal ultrasound - a twisted vascular pedicle seen as a round hypoechoic structure with concentric internal echoes - is the most specific ultrasound finding for ovarian torsion, with specificity exceeding 95%.

sources.label: RCOG - Management of Ovarian Cysts in Pregnancy

stem: A 30-year-old woman at 29 weeks gestation presents with a gush of clear fluid from the vagina 2 hours ago. Sterile speculum examination reveals pooling of clear fluid in the posterior fornix. AmniSure test is positive. She has no contractions, no vaginal bleeding, and no fever. Fetal heart rate on CTG is 145 bpm with normal variability and no decelerations. Group B Streptococcus status is unknown.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 80 bpm, BP 116/74 mmHg, Temp 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: WCC 10.2 x10^9/L, CRP 4 mg/L, urine MCS pending, low vaginal swab taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Immediate delivery by caesarean section given the risk of ascending infection at 29 weeks gestational age with ruptured membranes
options.rationale: At 29 weeks, the fetus is viable with good survival rates at tertiary centres. Immediate delivery would subject the neonate to significant prematurity-related morbidity. Expectant management with appropriate antibiotics and corticosteroids is the standard approach to gain time for fetal maturation while monitoring for complications. (Source: RANZCOG - PPROM)

options.text: Administer oral erythromycin 250 mg 6-hourly alone and plan delivery at 34 weeks if no complications arise in the interim
options.rationale: Erythromycin is appropriate prophylactic antibiotic therapy in PPROM (as per the ORACLE trial), but this answer omits the critical step of antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation. Additionally, without GBS status, GBS-specific intrapartum prophylaxis considerations are needed. (Source: RANZCOG - PPROM)

options.text: Commence IV amoxicillin and erythromycin for 48 hours then switch to oral, and administer corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation
options.rationale: This partially reflects the ORACLE protocol but is inaccurate. Australian practice follows erythromycin 250 mg 6-hourly for 10 days (or until delivery) as the prophylactic antibiotic. The amoxicillin-clavulanate combination was associated with increased necrotising enterocolitis risk in the ORACLE trial and should be avoided in PPROM. (Source: RANZCOG - PPROM)

options.text: Administer betamethasone 11.4 mg IM now and repeat in 24 hours, commence erythromycin 250 mg 6-hourly for 10 days, and manage expectantly
options.rationale: Management of PPROM at 29 weeks involves: (1) antenatal corticosteroids - betamethasone 11.4 mg IM two doses 24 hours apart for fetal lung maturation, (2) prophylactic antibiotics - erythromycin 250 mg orally 6-hourly for 10 days per the ORACLE trial protocol, to prolong latency and reduce neonatal infection, (3) expectant management with regular maternal observations, CTG monitoring, and ultrasound surveillance, and (4) planned delivery at 36-37 weeks if no complications, or earlier if chorioamnionitis, non-reassuring fetal status, or significant abruption develops. (Source: RANZCOG - PPROM)

options.text: Administer magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading dose for fetal neuroprotection, betamethasone for lungs, and plan delivery within 48 hours
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection is indicated when preterm delivery before 30 weeks is anticipated within 24 hours. This patient has PPROM without active labour, so delivery is not imminent. Planning delivery within 48 hours at 29 weeks would be premature when expectant management could safely extend the pregnancy by several weeks. (Source: RANZCOG - Magnesium Sulfate for Neuroprotection)

explanation.summary: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (PPROM) at 24-36 weeks is managed with expectant management to prolong the latency period and reduce prematurity-related morbidity. The key interventions are antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation (betamethasone 11.4 mg IM x 2 doses 24 hours apart), prophylactic erythromycin for 10 days to prolong latency and reduce neonatal infection, and careful maternal and fetal surveillance. Amoxicillin-clavulanate should be avoided due to the association with neonatal necrotising enterocolitis in the ORACLE trial. Delivery is planned at 36-37 weeks unless complications develop earlier.
key_points: Antenatal corticosteroids are given between 24 and 34+6 weeks to promote fetal lung maturation
Erythromycin 250 mg 6-hourly for 10 days is the prophylactic antibiotic of choice in PPROM
Amoxicillin-clavulanate is avoided in PPROM due to increased neonatal NEC risk from the ORACLE trial
Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection is given when delivery before 30 weeks is imminent
explanation.pearls: The ORACLE trial showed erythromycin in PPROM reduced neonatal morbidity and prolonged latency by a median of 5 days, but amoxicillin-clavulanate was associated with a 4.6-fold increase in neonatal necrotising enterocolitis - this combination should never be used in PPROM.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy is seen at 20 weeks gestation for a routine ultrasound. Twin 1 has a deepest vertical pocket of amniotic fluid of 1.8 cm with a collapsed-appearing bladder. Twin 2 has a deepest vertical pocket of 12 cm with a distended bladder. Both twins have concordant estimated fetal weights. Umbilical artery Dopplers are normal in both twins.

data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound - Twin 1: DVP 1.8 cm (oligohydramnios), bladder not visualised, EFW 320 g (50th centile). Twin 2: DVP 12 cm (polyhydramnios), distended bladder, EFW 330 g (50th centile). Placenta anterior, single shared mass

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat ultrasound in 2 weeks as the discordance may be transient and the Dopplers are currently reassuring
options.rationale: This twin pair meets diagnostic criteria for twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS): monochorionic pregnancy with oligohydramnios in the donor twin (DVP below 2 cm) and polyhydramnios in the recipient twin (DVP above 8 cm). TTTS is progressive and has high mortality without intervention. Waiting 2 weeks risks rapid deterioration. (Source: RANZCOG - Twin Pregnancy Management)

options.text: Amnioreduction of the polyhydramniotic sac to reduce the deepest vertical pocket below 8 cm and relieve symptoms
options.rationale: Amnioreduction was previously used as treatment for TTTS but only addresses the symptom (polyhydramnios), not the underlying pathology (unbalanced placental vascular anastomoses). The Eurofetus trial demonstrated superior outcomes with fetoscopic laser ablation compared with serial amnioreduction. Amnioreduction is reserved for cases where laser therapy is unavailable. (Source: RANZCOG - Twin Pregnancy Management)

options.text: Selective fetal reduction of the donor twin to protect the recipient from the complications of TTTS
options.rationale: Selective reduction is not appropriate when both twins are alive with normal growth and normal Dopplers. Fetoscopic laser ablation addresses the underlying vascular anastomoses and preserves both twins in the majority of cases (86% survival of at least one twin). Reduction is considered only when one twin has severe compromise. (Source: RANZCOG - Twin Pregnancy Management)

options.text: Immediate delivery by caesarean section at 20 weeks as the condition is not compatible with continued pregnancy
options.rationale: Delivery at 20 weeks results in the loss of both twins as the fetuses are previable. TTTS is treatable with fetoscopic laser ablation, which has survival rates of at least one twin in 86% and both twins in 60-70% of cases. The aim is to treat and prolong the pregnancy to a viable gestational age. (Source: RANZCOG - Twin Pregnancy Management)

options.text: Urgent referral to a fetal medicine centre for fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of placental vascular anastomoses
options.rationale: This presentation meets Quintero stage II TTTS criteria (oligohydramnios-polyhydramnios sequence with non-visualised donor bladder). Fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of the placental vascular anastomoses is the treatment of choice for TTTS diagnosed between 16 and 26 weeks, as demonstrated by the Eurofetus trial. The procedure uses a fetoscope inserted into the polyhydramniotic sac to identify and ablate the inter-twin vascular anastomoses on the placental surface. (Source: RANZCOG - Twin Pregnancy Management)

explanation.summary: Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome occurs in 10-15% of monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancies due to unbalanced blood flow through placental vascular anastomoses. The donor twin develops oligohydramnios and a small or absent bladder, while the recipient develops polyhydramnios and a distended bladder. The Quintero staging system classifies severity from stage I (fluid discordance only) to stage V (fetal demise). Fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of placental anastomoses is the treatment of choice between 16 and 26 weeks, with survival of at least one twin in approximately 86% of cases. All monochorionic twins require 2-weekly ultrasound surveillance from 16 weeks.
key_points: TTTS diagnostic criteria - DVP below 2 cm in donor and above 8 cm in recipient in monochorionic twins
Fetoscopic laser ablation is superior to serial amnioreduction (Eurofetus trial)
Quintero staging guides prognosis - stages I-II have better outcomes than stages III-IV
All monochorionic twins require 2-weekly ultrasound from 16 weeks for early TTTS detection
explanation.pearls: In the Quintero staging system for TTTS, a non-visualised donor bladder marks stage II, absent or reversed end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery marks stage III, and hydrops in either twin marks stage IV - each progressive stage carries significantly worse prognosis without intervention.

subtopic_detail: Vulval intraepithelial neoplasia and vulval cancer
stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with a 4-month history of a persistent, firm, raised vulval lesion on the left labium majus that has slowly enlarged. She reports intermittent pruritus and occasional bleeding when the lesion is irritated by clothing. She has a history of lichen sclerosus treated with topical clobetasol for 10 years. On examination, there is a 2.5 cm exophytic lesion on the left labium majus with irregular borders and contact bleeding. There are background white atrophic changes consistent with lichen sclerosus.

data_table.Examination: 2.5 cm firm exophytic lesion on left labium majus, irregular borders, contact bleeding, no palpable inguinofemoral lymphadenopathy, background lichen sclerosus changes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Punch biopsy of the lesion under local anaesthesia with referral to gynaecological oncology for results and management
options.rationale: A new or changing vulval lesion in the context of long-standing lichen sclerosus requires urgent biopsy to exclude vulval squamous cell carcinoma. Lichen sclerosus carries a 4-5% lifetime risk of vulval SCC, mediated through differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia (dVIN). A punch biopsy from the most suspicious area under local anaesthesia provides tissue diagnosis. Gynaecological oncology referral is essential for management planning. (Source: RANZCOG - Vulval Disease)

options.text: Increase clobetasol to daily application for 3 months as the lesion is likely a hypertrophic lichen sclerosus plaque
options.rationale: While lichen sclerosus can cause hyperkeratotic plaques, a new exophytic lesion with irregular borders and contact bleeding in long-standing lichen sclerosus must be biopsied to exclude malignancy before assuming a benign diagnosis. Treating empirically with potent topical steroids would delay diagnosis of a potentially invasive cancer. (Source: RANZCOG - Vulval Disease)

options.text: Wide local excision of the lesion with 1 cm margins as both diagnostic and therapeutic procedure at this visit
options.rationale: Proceeding directly to excision without a tissue diagnosis is inappropriate as the surgical margins and approach differ depending on histology (dVIN, microinvasive SCC, frankly invasive SCC). Punch biopsy first determines the diagnosis and depth of invasion, which guides definitive surgical planning including the need for sentinel lymph node biopsy or inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy. (Source: Cancer Council Australia - Vulval Cancer Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia - Vulval Cancer Guidelines

options.text: Apply topical imiquimod 5% cream three times weekly for 16 weeks for presumed HPV-related vulval intraepithelial neoplasia
options.rationale: Imiquimod is used for usual-type VIN (uVIN), which is HPV-related and typically occurs in younger women. This elderly patient with lichen sclerosus is at risk of differentiated VIN (dVIN) or invasive SCC, which is not HPV-related and does not respond to imiquimod. A tissue diagnosis is mandatory before any treatment. (Source: Cancer Council Australia - Vulval Cancer Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia - Vulval Cancer Guidelines

options.text: Arrange MRI of the pelvis and inguinal regions to stage the lesion before proceeding with any local intervention
options.rationale: Imaging may be needed for staging if the biopsy confirms invasive cancer, but it should not delay tissue diagnosis. The appropriate sequence is biopsy first, then imaging and staging investigations based on the histological result. For small vulval lesions, clinical examination of inguinal nodes is the initial assessment. (Source: Cancer Council Australia - Vulval Cancer Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia - Vulval Cancer Guidelines

explanation.summary: Vulval squamous cell carcinoma is the most common vulval malignancy, with two distinct pathways: HPV-related (via usual-type VIN in younger women) and HPV-independent (via differentiated VIN in older women, often associated with lichen sclerosus). Lichen sclerosus carries a 4-5% lifetime risk of SCC. Any new, persistent, or changing vulval lesion in a patient with lichen sclerosus requires biopsy. Management of confirmed vulval SCC involves wide local excision with appropriate margins and sentinel lymph node biopsy or inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy depending on depth of invasion. Women with lichen sclerosus require lifelong vulval surveillance.
key_points: Lichen sclerosus carries a 4-5% lifetime risk of vulval SCC via the dVIN pathway
Any new or changing vulval lesion in lichen sclerosus requires punch biopsy
dVIN is HPV-independent and does not respond to imiquimod, unlike usual-type VIN
Tissue diagnosis must precede definitive surgery to plan appropriate margins and lymph node assessment
explanation.pearls: Differentiated VIN (dVIN) associated with lichen sclerosus has a much higher malignant transformation rate (up to 30-50%) than HPV-related usual-type VIN (uVIN, approximately 5-10%), making vigilant long-term surveillance of lichen sclerosus essential.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia - Vulval Cancer Guidelines

stem: A 34-year-old woman at 7 weeks gestation following IVF with double embryo transfer presents with acute right iliac fossa pain and light vaginal spotting over the past 6 hours. She has no significant past medical history. Transvaginal ultrasound confirms a viable intrauterine pregnancy with fetal heart activity and a crown-rump length consistent with dates. A 28 mm right adnexal mass with a hyperechoic ring sign is identified, with moderate free fluid in the pouch of Douglas.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 104 bpm, BP 106/68 mmHg, T 36.9 C, RR 18, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: Right adnexal tenderness, guarding in right iliac fossa, cervix closed.
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG 48,000 IU/L, Hb 108 g/L, platelets 245 x10^9/L, group and save held.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Expectant management with serial beta-hCG levels every 48 hours
options.rationale: Expectant management is inappropriate here given haemodynamic compromise (tachycardia, borderline hypotension), free fluid suggesting rupture, and a sizeable adnexal mass. The ectopic component requires definitive surgical treatment. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Guidelines)

options.text: Urgent laparoscopic right salpingectomy preserving intrauterine pregnancy
options.rationale: Heterotopic pregnancy with signs of tubal rupture requires urgent surgical management. Laparoscopic salpingectomy removes the ectopic while preserving the viable intrauterine pregnancy. Methotrexate is absolutely contraindicated due to the coexisting viable IUP. The incidence of heterotopic pregnancy rises to 1-3% with ART. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Guidelines; RCOG Green-top Guideline 21)

options.text: Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate at 50 mg per square metre
options.rationale: Methotrexate is absolutely contraindicated in the presence of a viable intrauterine pregnancy as it is teratogenic and embryotoxic. Medical management of ectopic pregnancy is only appropriate when there is no coexisting IUP. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Guidelines)

options.text: Repeat transvaginal ultrasound in 48 hours to confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: Delaying intervention with a repeat scan is unsafe in a patient showing signs of haemoperitoneum with tachycardia and free fluid. The ultrasound findings already clearly demonstrate a heterotopic pregnancy with probable tubal rupture. (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline 21)

options.text: Laparotomy with bilateral salpingectomy and pregnancy termination
options.rationale: Bilateral salpingectomy with termination is unnecessarily radical. The goal is to remove the ectopic component while preserving the viable IUP. Laparoscopy is preferred over laparotomy when the patient is haemodynamically stable enough. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Heterotopic pregnancy occurs when intrauterine and ectopic pregnancies coexist. The incidence is approximately 1 in 30,000 in natural conception but rises to 1-3% with assisted reproduction, particularly with multiple embryo transfer. Management is exclusively surgical because methotrexate is contraindicated with a viable IUP. Laparoscopic salpingectomy is the standard approach when the patient is haemodynamically stable.
key_points: Heterotopic pregnancy incidence is 1-3% after IVF with multiple embryo transfer
Methotrexate is absolutely contraindicated with a coexisting viable IUP
Laparoscopic salpingectomy is preferred over laparotomy when feasible
Free fluid and tachycardia suggest tubal rupture requiring urgent intervention
explanation.pearls: After surgical management of a heterotopic pregnancy, the intrauterine pregnancy continues successfully in approximately 65-70% of cases, with outcomes improving when intervention occurs before significant haemoperitoneum develops.

subtopic_detail: Interpreting the day 4 to day 7 hCG change after methotrexate
stem: A 30-year-old woman was given intramuscular methotrexate seven days ago for a tubal ectopic pregnancy. She has mild intermittent left iliac fossa discomfort, no dizziness and no shoulder tip pain. Her abdomen is soft.

data_table.Serum hCG: Day 0: 2,600 IU/L; day 4: 2,900 IU/L; day 7: 2,700 IU/L
data_table.Investigations: Hb 126 g/L; creatinine 64 micromol/L; ALT 24 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give a second dose of intramuscular methotrexate today
options.rationale: A fall of less than 15 per cent between day 4 and day 7 defines an inadequate response, and about one woman in seven needs a further dose with the monitoring cycle repeated from that day. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Repeat the hCG in one week without any further treatment
options.rationale: Weekly monitoring alone is what follows an adequate day 4 to day 7 fall, and it continues until the level is undetectable. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Arrange laparoscopic salpingectomy on the emergency list
options.rationale: Emergency surgery is for haemodynamic compromise, significant free fluid with peritonism, or failure after a second dose; she is stable with mild pain. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Admit for intravenous methotrexate over the next 24 hours
options.rationale: Intravenous methotrexate belongs to oncological and rheumatological regimens with folinic acid rescue, and has no place in tubal ectopic pregnancy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetrics)

options.text: Begin a course of oral mifepristone and then misoprostol
options.rationale: Mifepristone with misoprostol is the regimen for medical termination of an intrauterine pregnancy and does not treat trophoblast implanted in the tube. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetrics)

explanation.summary: After single dose methotrexate the hCG usually rises to a peak around day 4, so that rise is expected and is not treatment failure. The decision point is the change between day 4 and day 7: a fall of at least 15 per cent means the treatment is working and weekly hCG continues until it is undetectable, while a smaller fall or a rise means a second dose, with day 4 and day 7 measured again from that injection. Surgery follows failure of the second dose or any clinical deterioration. In context, methotrexate is not a single visit treatment; a woman who cannot commit to the follow-up schedule is better served by laparoscopic surgery from the outset.
key_points: An hCG rise from day 0 to day 4 is expected and is not failure.
At least a 15 per cent fall from day 4 to day 7 means treatment is working.
A smaller fall or a rise means a second dose and a fresh day 4 and day 7 cycle.
Weekly hCG continues until undetectable; about one in seven needs a second dose.
explanation.pearls: Advise avoiding alcohol, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, folate supplements and sun exposure during treatment, and no conception until three months after the last dose.

sources.label: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

stem:
A 36-year-old G3P2 woman at 37 weeks gestation presents with 4 days of progressive dyspnoea, now orthopnoeic with a dry cough. She was seen 48 hours ago by her GP who attributed the symptoms to the late third trimester. She has no history of hypertension or cardiac disease. Her two prior pregnancies were uncomplicated vaginal deliveries. On arrival she is sitting upright, visibly distressed, and unable to complete sentences.

Auscultation reveals bilateral basal crackles to the mid-zones and a third heart sound. There is no peripheral oedema beyond mild ankle swelling. Her blood pressure is 124/78 mmHg and urinalysis shows no proteinuria. Bedside echocardiography demonstrates a left ventricular ejection fraction of 28% with global hypokinesis and no valvular pathology.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg, RR 32, SpO2 88% on room air, T 36.6 C.
data_table.Investigations: NT-proBNP 8,400 pg/mL, troponin I 0.08 ng/mL (ULN 0.04), Hb 122 g/L, platelets 234 x10^9/L, ALT 32 U/L, creatinine 72 micromol/L, urine PCR < 10 mg/mmol. CTG: reassuring with no decelerations.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management priority?

options.text: Commence IV magnesium sulfate infusion and plan urgent caesarean delivery
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is indicated for seizure prophylaxis in pre-eclampsia or eclampsia. This patient has no hypertension, no proteinuria, normal platelets, and normal LFTs, making pre-eclampsia unlikely. The echo findings of LVEF 28% point to a primary cardiac pathology. Magnesium could worsen cardiac output. (Source: SOMANZ Guidelines; NHFA Heart Failure Guidelines)

options.text: Administer IV labetalol 20 mg for blood pressure control and monitor closely
options.rationale: Labetalol is appropriate for hypertensive emergencies in pregnancy, but this patient's blood pressure is 124/78 mmHg and does not require antihypertensive therapy. Beta-blockers must also be used cautiously in acute decompensated heart failure as they can worsen cardiogenic shock. (Source: NHFA Heart Failure Guidelines)

options.text: Commence high-flow oxygen and arrange urgent induction of labour with oxytocin
options.rationale: While delivery is ultimately beneficial in peripartum cardiomyopathy, this patient requires immediate cardiac stabilisation before any delivery planning. Oxytocin also has antidiuretic effects and can cause fluid retention, which could worsen pulmonary oedema in a patient with severely reduced LVEF. (Source: NHFA Heart Failure Guidelines)

options.text: Commence IV furosemide and oxygen with urgent cardiology and obstetric review
options.rationale: This patient has peripartum cardiomyopathy presenting with acute decompensated heart failure. The immediate priority is haemodynamic stabilisation with IV diuresis for pulmonary oedema, supplemental oxygen for hypoxia, and urgent joint cardiology-obstetric review. LVEF of 28% with elevated NT-proBNP, third heart sound, and bilateral crackles confirm cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. Delivery timing is a joint decision after stabilisation. (Source: NHFA Heart Failure Guidelines; ESC Peripartum Cardiomyopathy Position Statement)

options.text: Urgent CT pulmonary angiogram to exclude massive pulmonary embolism first
options.rationale: While PE is on the differential for peripartum dyspnoea, the bedside echo showing LVEF 28% with global hypokinesis and a third heart sound already identifies the diagnosis. CTPA would delay treatment, expose mother and fetus to radiation unnecessarily, and the echo findings are not consistent with right heart strain from PE. (Source: NHFA Heart Failure Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is a diagnosis of exclusion defined as heart failure with LVEF below 45% developing in the last month of pregnancy or within 5 months postpartum. It can mimic pre-eclampsia with dyspnoea and oedema, but the absence of hypertension, proteinuria, and hepatic or haematological derangement distinguishes the two. Immediate management focuses on stabilising heart failure before delivery planning. Long-term prognosis depends on LVEF recovery, with approximately 50% of patients recovering normal function within 6 months.
key_points: PPCM is defined as LVEF < 45% in late pregnancy or early postpartum with no prior cardiac disease
Normal BP and absent proteinuria distinguish PPCM from pre-eclampsia with pulmonary oedema
IV furosemide and oxygen are first-line for acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema in pregnancy
Delivery timing requires joint cardiology-obstetric decision after haemodynamic stabilisation
explanation.pearls: Bromocriptine 2.5 mg twice daily for 2 weeks then 2.5 mg daily for 6 weeks has shown promise in improving LVEF recovery in peripartum cardiomyopathy by blocking the pro-apoptotic 16 kDa prolactin fragment, though it requires cessation of breastfeeding.

subtopic_detail: Antiphospholipid syndrome in recurrent pregnancy loss
stem: A 31-year-old woman attends the recurrent miscarriage clinic after three consecutive first-trimester losses, all between 8 and 10 weeks gestation. She has no living children. Investigations reveal persistently positive lupus anticoagulant on two occasions 14 weeks apart and anticardiolipin IgG at 62 GPL units (positive > 40). Her partner's karyotype and her own are normal. Thyroid function, glucose tolerance, and uterine cavity assessment by saline infusion sonography are all normal. She is now 6 weeks pregnant again, confirmed by ultrasound showing an intrauterine gestational sac with a yolk sac.

data_table.Investigations: Lupus anticoagulant: positive (confirmed on two occasions 14 weeks apart). Anticardiolipin IgG: 62 GPL (positive > 40). Anti-beta2 glycoprotein I IgG: negative. FBC, UEC, LFTs, TFTs: normal. OGTT: normal. Parental karyotypes: normal.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment for this pregnancy?

options.text: Low-dose aspirin 150 mg daily alone without any anticoagulation therapy
options.rationale: Aspirin alone is insufficient for obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome with recurrent pregnancy loss. The combination of aspirin plus heparin has been shown to significantly improve live birth rates compared with aspirin alone in APS-associated recurrent miscarriage. (Source: RANZCOG APS in Pregnancy; RCOG Green-top Guideline 17)

options.text: Therapeutic-dose enoxaparin 1.5 mg per kg daily without additional aspirin
options.rationale: Therapeutic-dose anticoagulation is indicated for APS with prior thrombotic events, not for purely obstetric APS without thrombotic history. Prophylactic-dose enoxaparin combined with aspirin is the standard for obstetric APS. Therapeutic dosing increases bleeding risk without proven additional benefit for pregnancy outcomes. (Source: RANZCOG APS in Pregnancy)

options.text: Low-dose aspirin 150 mg daily plus prophylactic enoxaparin 40 mg daily
options.rationale: The standard of care for obstetric APS with recurrent pregnancy loss is the combination of low-dose aspirin (commenced preconception or at positive pregnancy test) plus prophylactic-dose low-molecular-weight heparin (e.g. enoxaparin 40 mg daily) commenced once a viable intrauterine pregnancy is confirmed. This combination improves live birth rates from approximately 40% to 70-80%. (Source: RANZCOG APS in Pregnancy; RCOG Green-top Guideline 17)

options.text: Warfarin at a target INR of 2.0 to 3.0 throughout the entire pregnancy
options.rationale: Warfarin is teratogenic in the first trimester (causing warfarin embryopathy between 6 and 12 weeks) and is contraindicated in the first trimester and near term. It is replaced by LMWH in pregnancy. Warfarin may only be considered mid-trimester in women with mechanical heart valves. (Source: RANZCOG APS in Pregnancy)

options.text: Prednisolone 20 mg daily plus low-dose aspirin throughout the pregnancy
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are not recommended for obstetric APS. Trials showed no benefit for pregnancy outcomes and increased maternal morbidity including gestational diabetes, hypertension, and preterm birth. The combination of aspirin plus heparin has superior evidence. (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline 17)

explanation.summary: Antiphospholipid syndrome is diagnosed when at least one clinical criterion (vascular thrombosis or pregnancy morbidity) and at least one laboratory criterion (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, or anti-beta2 glycoprotein I antibodies confirmed on two occasions at least 12 weeks apart) are met. In obstetric APS with recurrent pregnancy loss, aspirin plus prophylactic LMWH is the standard treatment, improving live birth rates substantially. Close antenatal surveillance including serial growth scans and uterine artery Doppler is recommended due to increased risk of pre-eclampsia and placental insufficiency.
key_points: Diagnosis requires clinical plus laboratory criteria with antibodies confirmed 12 weeks apart
Aspirin plus prophylactic LMWH is standard for obstetric APS without prior thrombosis
Warfarin is teratogenic in the first trimester and contraindicated
These pregnancies require surveillance for pre-eclampsia, FGR, and placental abruption
explanation.pearls: Triple-positive APS (positive lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, and anti-beta2 glycoprotein I) carries the highest thrombotic risk and worst obstetric outcomes, with some experts advocating for higher-intensity anticoagulation in this subgroup despite limited trial evidence.

stem: A 26-year-old G2P1 woman at 9 weeks gestation presents with heavy vaginal bleeding and cramping lower abdominal pain for 6 hours. She has soaked through four pads in the last 2 hours. She is Rh-negative. On examination, the cervical os is open with products of conception visible at the os. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an intrauterine gestational sac containing a fetal pole with no cardiac activity and a crown-rump length of 18 mm. She is haemodynamically stable and wishes active management to resolve the miscarriage quickly.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 94 bpm, BP 112/72 mmHg, T 36.8 C.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 116 g/L, blood group A Rh-negative, no irregular antibodies detected.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Oral mifepristone 200 mg followed by misoprostol 800 mcg in 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: Mifepristone-misoprostol is the medical management regimen for missed miscarriage when the cervix is closed. In inevitable miscarriage with an open os and products visible, surgical evacuation is more appropriate, particularly with heavy ongoing bleeding. Medical management risks prolonged bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG Early Pregnancy Loss Guidelines)

options.text: Surgical evacuation of retained products plus anti-D immunoglobulin 250 IU
options.rationale: This patient has an inevitable miscarriage (open os, products visible, no cardiac activity) with heavy bleeding and a preference for rapid resolution. Surgical evacuation is the most appropriate active management. As she is Rh-negative and beyond 10 weeks by CRL sizing, anti-D immunoglobulin is required to prevent Rh isoimmunisation. At less than 12 weeks, the dose is 250 IU. (Source: RANZCOG Early Pregnancy Loss Guidelines; ANZSBT Anti-D Guidelines)

options.text: Expectant management with review in one week and serial beta-hCG levels
options.rationale: While expectant management is an option for some miscarriages, this patient has heavy bleeding with products at the os and has expressed a preference for active management. Expectant management would prolong her symptoms and carries a risk of incomplete miscarriage and infection. (Source: NICE NG126: Ectopic Pregnancy and Miscarriage)
source_refs: NICE NG126: Ectopic Pregnancy and Miscarriage

options.text: Vaginal misoprostol 800 mcg alone without prior mifepristone as a single dose
options.rationale: While misoprostol alone can be used for medical management of miscarriage, surgical evacuation is preferred when products are already at the os and bleeding is heavy. Medical management alone has a higher incomplete evacuation rate and would not address the patient's preference for rapid resolution. (Source: RANZCOG Early Pregnancy Loss Guidelines)

options.text: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV plus oxytocin infusion to reduce bleeding and observe
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid and oxytocin may reduce bleeding symptomatically but do not address the retained products of conception. Definitive management requires either surgical or medical evacuation. Temporising with uterotonics alone risks incomplete miscarriage and sepsis. (Source: RANZCOG Early Pregnancy Loss Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Inevitable miscarriage is characterised by an open cervical os with or without products of conception visible, often with heavy bleeding. Management options include surgical evacuation, medical management, or expectant management. Patient preference and clinical circumstances guide the choice. Rh-negative women require anti-D immunoglobulin after any pregnancy loss to prevent isoimmunisation in future pregnancies. The dose depends on gestational age: 250 IU before 12 weeks and 625 IU at or after 12 weeks in Australia.
key_points: Open os with products visible defines inevitable miscarriage
Surgical evacuation is preferred for heavy bleeding and patient preference for rapid resolution
Anti-D 250 IU is required for Rh-negative women losing a pregnancy before 12 weeks
All three management options are valid but clinical context guides selection
explanation.pearls: Anti-D immunoglobulin is not required for threatened miscarriage before 12 weeks unless bleeding is heavy, recurrent, or associated with abdominal pain, but it IS required for all complete, incomplete, and inevitable miscarriages regardless of gestational age in Rh-negative women.

sources.label: NICE NG126: Ectopic Pregnancy and Miscarriage

subtopic_detail: Menopausal hormone therapy route and VTE risk
stem: A 52-year-old woman presents with severe vasomotor symptoms including 12 to 15 hot flushes daily and significant sleep disturbance for the past 8 months since her last menstrual period. Her FSH is 68 IU/L confirming menopause. She has a BMI of 36 kg per square metre, a personal history of provoked deep vein thrombosis following knee arthroscopy 3 years ago (completed 3 months of rivaroxaban, now off anticoagulation), and well-controlled hypertension on amlodipine. She has an intact uterus. Lifestyle measures have been insufficient. She is requesting hormonal treatment for her symptoms.

data_table.Investigations: FSH 68 IU/L, oestradiol < 100 pmol/L, TSH 2.4 mIU/L, FBC normal, LFTs normal, lipid profile: total cholesterol 5.8 mmol/L, LDL 3.4 mmol/L, HDL 1.2 mmol/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate hormonal treatment approach?

options.text: Oral conjugated equine oestrogen 0.625 mg daily plus oral medroxyprogesterone
options.rationale: Oral oestrogen undergoes first-pass hepatic metabolism, which increases hepatic synthesis of clotting factors and raises VTE risk 2-4 fold. In a woman with prior VTE and BMI over 35, oral oestrogen is relatively contraindicated due to compounding thrombotic risk factors. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT)

options.text: Oral tibolone 2.5 mg daily as a combined oestrogenic and progestogenic agent
options.rationale: Tibolone, while having fewer oestrogenic effects on coagulation than conjugated oestrogens, is still an oral agent with first-pass metabolism. Its VTE risk profile in women with prior thrombotic events is not sufficiently reassuring compared to transdermal oestradiol, which avoids hepatic first-pass entirely. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT)

options.text: Venlafaxine 75 mg daily as a non-hormonal alternative for vasomotor symptoms
options.rationale: Non-hormonal options such as venlafaxine can reduce hot flush frequency by approximately 50-60%, but this patient is specifically requesting hormonal treatment and her symptoms are severe. A safer hormonal route exists that avoids the VTE risk of oral oestrogen. Non-hormonal therapy should be reserved for absolute contraindications. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT)

options.text: Oral oestradiol valerate 2 mg daily plus micronised progesterone 100 mg daily
options.rationale: Although micronised progesterone is the preferred progestogen for metabolic safety, the oral oestradiol component still carries the first-pass hepatic VTE risk. In a woman with prior VTE and obesity, the oestrogen route must be transdermal rather than oral, regardless of which progestogen is chosen. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT)

options.text: Transdermal oestradiol 50 mcg patch plus oral micronised progesterone nightly
options.rationale: Transdermal oestradiol bypasses hepatic first-pass metabolism and does not increase VTE risk, making it the preferred route in women with prior VTE or elevated thrombotic risk. Observational data consistently show no increased VTE risk with transdermal oestradiol at standard doses. Micronised progesterone is the preferred progestogen as it has the most favourable safety profile for VTE, breast, and cardiovascular outcomes. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT; Lancet 2019 meta-analysis)

explanation.summary: Menopausal hormone therapy route selection is critical in women with VTE risk factors. Transdermal oestradiol avoids hepatic first-pass metabolism and therefore does not increase clotting factor synthesis or VTE risk. This contrasts with oral oestrogen, which increases VTE risk 2-4 fold through hepatic effects. Micronised progesterone is preferred over synthetic progestogens for its more favourable safety profile. Women with a prior VTE are not absolutely contraindicated from MHT if the transdermal route is used, though shared decision-making with a haematologist may be advisable.
key_points: Transdermal oestradiol avoids first-pass hepatic metabolism and does not increase VTE risk
Oral oestrogen increases VTE risk 2-4 fold via hepatic clotting factor synthesis
Micronised progesterone has the lowest VTE risk among progestogens
Prior provoked VTE is a relative, not absolute, contraindication to transdermal MHT
explanation.pearls: The ESTHER and E3N French cohort studies demonstrated that transdermal oestradiol combined with micronised progesterone carried no measurable increase in VTE risk (OR 0.9, 95% CI 0.5-1.6), even in women with BMI above 30 or thrombophilia.

subtopic_detail: Management of cervical screening abnormality during pregnancy
stem: A 30-year-old G1P0 woman at 14 weeks gestation has her routine cervical screening test result return as HPV 16 positive with a low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion on liquid-based cytology. She had a normal cervical screening test 3 years ago. She is well with no vaginal bleeding or discharge. She has no history of abnormal cervical screening and is a non-smoker.

data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening: HPV 16 detected. LBC: low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL).

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Colposcopy during pregnancy without biopsy unless high-grade disease suspected
options.rationale: HPV 16 positivity with any cytological abnormality requires colposcopy. Colposcopy is safe in pregnancy and should be performed to exclude high-grade disease. Biopsy is reserved for suspected high-grade or invasive lesions only, as routine biopsy risks bleeding from the hypervascular cervix. Treatment is deferred until postpartum. (Source: NCSP Guidelines; RANZCOG Cervical Screening in Pregnancy)

options.text: Defer all investigation until 6 weeks postpartum for repeat cervical screen
options.rationale: HPV 16 is the highest-risk HPV genotype and deferring all investigation until postpartum risks missing an underlying high-grade lesion or early invasive carcinoma. Colposcopy should be performed during pregnancy to exclude serious pathology, even though treatment is deferred. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

options.text: Immediate large loop excision of the transformation zone under local anaesthesia
options.rationale: LLETZ is contraindicated during pregnancy due to the risk of haemorrhage from the hypervascular pregnant cervix, cervical incompetence, preterm rupture of membranes, and pregnancy loss. Excisional treatment is deferred to at least 3 months postpartum. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Screening in Pregnancy)

options.text: Repeat cervical screening in 12 months as HPV 16 with LSIL is low risk
options.rationale: HPV 16 with any cytological abnormality is not low risk. HPV 16 has the highest oncogenic potential of all HPV genotypes and requires direct colposcopic assessment regardless of the cytology grade. A 12-month repeat would be inappropriate for this high-risk genotype. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

options.text: Cervical biopsy under ultrasound guidance to obtain histological confirmation
options.rationale: Ultrasound-guided cervical biopsy is not a standard technique for cervical screening follow-up. Colposcopy is the standard assessment method. Biopsy during pregnancy is performed only under colposcopic guidance when a high-grade or invasive lesion is suspected. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

explanation.summary: The Australian National Cervical Screening Program recommends colposcopy for any HPV 16 or 18 detection regardless of cytology result. Colposcopy is safe during pregnancy and should be performed to exclude invasive disease. Routine biopsies are avoided due to bleeding risk from cervical hypervascularity, but directed biopsies are taken if high-grade or invasive disease is suspected. Treatment with excisional procedures is deferred until at least 3 months postpartum, with repeat colposcopy recommended at that time.
key_points: HPV 16 or 18 detection mandates colposcopy regardless of cytology grade
Colposcopy is safe in pregnancy; treatment is deferred postpartum
Biopsy only if high-grade or invasive disease is colposcopically suspected
LLETZ is contraindicated during pregnancy due to haemorrhage and cervical incompetence risk
explanation.pearls: HPV 16 is responsible for approximately 55-60% of all cervical cancers and has a 12% 10-year risk of CIN3+ even when the initial cytology is normal, which is why the NCSP mandates colposcopy for HPV 16 regardless of cytology.

stem: A 54-year-old woman who underwent total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy 6 months ago for heavy menstrual bleeding due to fibroids is experiencing significant vasomotor symptoms with 10 hot flushes daily, severe night sweats, and insomnia. She has well-controlled hypertension on perindopril and no personal or family history of breast cancer or VTE. Her BMI is 27 kg per square metre. She is requesting hormone therapy for symptom relief. Her baseline mammogram performed 4 months ago was normal.

data_table.Investigations: FSH 82 IU/L, TSH 2.1 mIU/L, lipid profile normal, mammogram (4 months ago): BI-RADS 1.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate hormone therapy regimen?

options.text: Combined continuous oestradiol and micronised progesterone daily long-term
options.rationale: A progestogen is only required to protect the endometrium from unopposed oestrogen. This patient has had a total hysterectomy and therefore has no endometrium. Adding progesterone unnecessarily increases breast cancer risk and side effects without benefit. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT)

options.text: Cyclical combined oestradiol for 25 days with progesterone for the last 14
options.rationale: Cyclical combined therapy produces a withdrawal bleed and is used in perimenopausal women with an intact uterus who prefer to menstruate regularly. This patient has no uterus, so cyclical progesterone is unnecessary and the withdrawal bleeds would be impossible. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT)

options.text: Tibolone 2.5 mg daily as it combines oestrogenic and progestogenic activity
options.rationale: Tibolone is an option for postmenopausal symptom relief, but it is not first-line. In a woman post-hysterectomy, the combined oestrogenic-progestogenic properties of tibolone provide no advantage over oestrogen alone, and tibolone carries a small increased stroke risk in older women. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT)

options.text: Oestradiol-only therapy either as transdermal patch or oral tablet daily
options.rationale: After total hysterectomy with bilateral oophorectomy, oestrogen-only therapy is appropriate as there is no endometrium to protect. Oestrogen-only MHT provides effective symptom relief with a more favourable risk profile than combined therapy, including lower breast cancer risk. Either oral or transdermal route is acceptable in this patient without VTE risk factors. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT; WHI oestrogen-only arm)

options.text: Vaginal oestrogen pessary alone for both vasomotor and urogenital symptoms
options.rationale: Vaginal oestrogen is effective for urogenital atrophy symptoms but provides negligible systemic absorption and is insufficient for treating moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms. Systemic oestrogen therapy is required for hot flushes and night sweats. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT)

explanation.summary: Women who have undergone hysterectomy do not require a progestogen component in their MHT, as the sole purpose of progesterone is endometrial protection from unopposed oestrogen. Oestrogen-only therapy is preferred post-hysterectomy because it avoids the additional breast cancer risk associated with combined therapy. The WHI oestrogen-only arm demonstrated no increased breast cancer risk over 7 years of follow-up, in contrast to the combined arm.
key_points: Oestrogen-only MHT is appropriate after hysterectomy as no endometrial protection is needed
Adding progesterone post-hysterectomy increases breast cancer risk without benefit
The WHI oestrogen-only arm showed no increased breast cancer risk
Route selection depends on VTE risk factors and patient preference
explanation.pearls: The WHI oestrogen-only arm (conjugated equine oestrogen 0.625 mg daily) showed a non-significant 23% reduction in breast cancer incidence over 7 years (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.59-1.01), contrasting sharply with the 26% increase seen in the combined oestrogen-progestogen arm.

stem:
A 28-year-old woman with polycystic ovary syndrome diagnosed at age 22 presents for review. She has oligomenorrhoea with 4 to 5 cycles per year and moderate hirsutism. She is not currently trying to conceive and uses condoms for contraception. Her BMI is 34 kg per square metre, having gained 12 kg over the past 3 years. She has acanthosis nigricans at the neck and axillae.

An oral glucose tolerance test shows a fasting glucose of 5.8 mmol/L and a 2-hour glucose of 9.4 mmol/L. Her HbA1c is 42 mmol per mol. Fasting lipids show total cholesterol 5.9 mmol/L, triglycerides 2.8 mmol/L, HDL 0.9 mmol/L, and LDL 3.6 mmol/L. She asks which intervention is most important for her long-term health.

data_table.Investigations: OGTT: fasting 5.8 mmol/L, 2-hour 9.4 mmol/L. HbA1c 42 mmol/mol. Lipids: TC 5.9, TG 2.8, HDL 0.9, LDL 3.6 mmol/L. Testosterone 3.2 nmol/L (ULN 1.8). SHBG 18 nmol/L (low). LH 14 IU/L, FSH 5 IU/L.

lead_in: What is the single most important initial management priority?

options.text: Structured lifestyle intervention targeting 5-10% weight loss over 6 months
options.rationale: The 2023 international evidence-based PCOS guideline identifies structured lifestyle intervention with 5-10% weight loss as the first-line treatment for all metabolic features of PCOS. A 5% weight loss can restore ovulation, improve insulin sensitivity, reduce testosterone, and improve the lipid profile. This patient has impaired glucose tolerance (2-hour glucose 7.8-11.0 mmol/L) and dyslipidaemia, both of which respond to weight management. (Source: International PCOS Guideline 2023; Jean Hailes for Women's Health)

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill for cycle regulation and androgen suppression
options.rationale: The COCP addresses menstrual irregularity and hirsutism but does not address the metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, or impaired glucose tolerance which represent the greatest long-term health risks. With a BMI of 34 and metabolic syndrome features, lifestyle intervention takes priority. The COCP may also worsen insulin resistance and lipid profile. (Source: International PCOS Guideline 2023)

options.text: Metformin 500 mg twice daily titrated to 1 g twice daily for insulin resistance
options.rationale: Metformin can improve insulin sensitivity and may modestly aid weight loss, but international guidelines position it as second-line to lifestyle intervention. Metformin alone without lifestyle change produces modest improvements in metabolic parameters. It may be added if lifestyle intervention alone is insufficient after 3-6 months. (Source: International PCOS Guideline 2023)

options.text: Spironolactone 50 mg twice daily for hyperandrogenism and hirsutism control
options.rationale: Spironolactone is effective for hirsutism and acne but does not address the metabolic complications which are this patient's greatest long-term health concern. It also requires reliable contraception due to teratogenicity. Cosmetic symptoms, while distressing, are secondary to metabolic risk reduction. (Source: International PCOS Guideline 2023)

options.text: Atorvastatin 20 mg daily for dyslipidaemia and cardiovascular risk reduction
options.rationale: Statin therapy may be considered for dyslipidaemia but is not the most important initial intervention in a 28-year-old with PCOS. Lifestyle intervention can substantially improve the lipid profile and address the underlying insulin resistance driving the dyslipidaemia. Statins also require reliable contraception. (Source: International PCOS Guideline 2023)

explanation.summary: PCOS is a metabolic as well as reproductive disorder. Women with PCOS have a 4-8 fold increased risk of type 2 diabetes compared to age-matched controls. The 2023 international evidence-based guideline emphasises lifestyle intervention as the cornerstone of PCOS management, particularly when metabolic features are present. A 5-10% weight reduction can restore ovulation in up to 60% of anovulatory women with PCOS and significantly improves insulin sensitivity, lipid profile, and cardiovascular risk markers.
key_points: Lifestyle intervention with 5-10% weight loss is first-line for all metabolic features of PCOS
OGTT 2-hour glucose of 9.4 mmol/L indicates impaired glucose tolerance (prediabetes)
Metabolic risk reduction takes priority over cosmetic symptoms like hirsutism
Metformin is second-line, added if lifestyle alone is insufficient after 3-6 months
explanation.pearls: Annual OGTT screening is recommended for all women with PCOS and BMI over 25 (or other risk factors), as HbA1c underestimates glycaemic impairment in PCOS due to the younger age demographic and may miss up to 50% of cases of impaired glucose tolerance.

stem: A 24-year-old nulliparous woman presents with a 3-year history of worsening dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, and chronic pelvic pain. Pain is worst in the 2 days before and during menstruation. She rates her pain as 8 out of 10 during menses despite regular paracetamol and ibuprofen. She is not currently planning pregnancy. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 25 mm left ovarian endometrioma but is otherwise unremarkable. She has not tried hormonal therapy previously.

data_table.Investigations: TVUS: 25 mm left ovarian endometrioma with ground-glass appearance. Uterus normal. Right ovary normal. No evidence of deep infiltrating endometriosis on ultrasound.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial medical treatment?

options.text: GnRH agonist depot injection monthly with add-back oestrogen therapy
options.rationale: GnRH agonists are second-line therapy for endometriosis, reserved for patients who fail first-line hormonal suppression. They cause significant hypo-oestrogenic side effects and require add-back therapy. They should not be used as initial treatment in a young woman who has not tried simpler hormonal options. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Guidelines; NICE NG73)

options.text: Laparoscopic excision of the endometrioma and ablation of peritoneal disease
options.rationale: Surgery is not first-line for endometriosis management when the patient has not tried hormonal suppression. For a 25 mm endometrioma without fertility concerns, medical management should be attempted first. Surgery is appropriate for failed medical therapy, fertility planning, or diagnostic uncertainty. (Source: ESHRE Endometriosis Guideline 2022)

options.text: Oral danazol 200 mg twice daily for suppression of endometrial implants
options.rationale: Danazol is effective for endometriosis but is rarely used as first-line therapy due to androgenic side effects including acne, hirsutism, weight gain, and voice deepening. Modern first-line options have far better tolerability profiles. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Guidelines)

options.text: Medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg IM every 12 weeks as depot injection
options.rationale: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate is effective for endometriosis pain but carries significant concerns about bone mineral density loss with prolonged use, particularly in young women. It is also associated with weight gain and irregular bleeding. It is not preferred as first-line in a 24-year-old. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Guidelines)

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill taken continuously to suppress menstruation
options.rationale: Continuous combined oral contraceptive pill is recommended as first-line medical therapy for endometriosis-related pain in women not planning pregnancy. Continuous use eliminates withdrawal bleeds and provides sustained suppression of oestrogenic stimulation of endometrial implants. It is well tolerated, inexpensive, and provides contraception. A levonorgestrel IUD is an equivalent first-line alternative. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Guidelines; ESHRE Endometriosis Guideline 2022)

explanation.summary: Endometriosis affects approximately 10% of reproductive-age women. First-line medical management is hormonal suppression using the combined oral contraceptive pill taken continuously or a levonorgestrel intrauterine device. These suppress ovulation and decidualise endometrial implants, reducing pain in approximately 70-80% of patients. Second-line options include progestogen-only therapies and GnRH agonists. Surgical management is reserved for failed medical therapy, fertility planning, or diagnostic uncertainty.
key_points: COCP taken continuously is first-line medical therapy for endometriosis pain
LNG-IUD is an equivalent first-line alternative
GnRH agonists and danazol are second-line due to side effect profiles
Surgery is not first-line when hormonal suppression has not been tried
explanation.pearls: Continuous COCP use for endometriosis should genuinely suppress menstruation with no scheduled breaks; the traditional 21/7 cyclical regimen allows hormonal withdrawal that can reactivate endometrial implants and worsen pain during the pill-free interval.

stem: A 33-year-old G2P1 woman at 31 weeks and 4 days gestation is admitted with epigastric pain, nausea, and malaise over 24 hours. Her blood pressure is 158/102 mmHg on two readings 15 minutes apart. She has brisk reflexes without clonus. Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 48 mg/mmol. Blood results show evidence of haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets consistent with HELLP syndrome. The CTG is reassuring. Estimated fetal weight on recent growth scan is on the 32nd centile with normal umbilical artery Doppler.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 158/102 mmHg, HR 96 bpm, T 37.0 C, RR 18.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 98 g/L (was 118 at 28 weeks), platelets 68 x10^9/L, blood film: schistocytes and helmet cells, LDH 620 U/L, haptoglobin < 0.1 g/L, ALT 248 U/L, AST 312 U/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, urate 0.44 mmol/L, urine PCR 48 mg/mmol, fibrinogen 2.8 g/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Immediate caesarean section without corticosteroids given the HELLP diagnosis
options.rationale: At 31 weeks, antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity should be administered if delivery can be safely delayed 24-48 hours. HELLP syndrome is an indication for delivery but not necessarily immediate delivery if the patient is stable. The window for corticosteroid benefit should be utilised where possible. (Source: SOMANZ Guidelines; RANZCOG Fetal Surveillance Guideline)

options.text: Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM now with planned delivery within 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: At 31 weeks with HELLP syndrome, the management priority is to administer corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity while planning delivery within 24-48 hours. The patient is currently stable (no DIC, no hepatic haematoma, no eclampsia, reassuring CTG) allowing a short window for steroid benefit. Antihypertensives should be commenced concurrently. Close monitoring of platelets, LFTs, and maternal status every 6-12 hours is essential. (Source: SOMANZ Guidelines; RCOG Green-top Guideline 10A)

options.text: Expectant management with IV dexamethasone to reverse the HELLP process
options.rationale: Dexamethasone for HELLP reversal (as opposed to fetal lung maturity) was studied but has not shown consistent benefit in randomised trials. Expectant management beyond the 24-48 hours needed for fetal corticosteroids is not recommended in HELLP syndrome due to the risk of rapid deterioration including hepatic rupture, DIC, and placental abruption. (Source: SOMANZ Guidelines)

options.text: Urgent platelet transfusion to above 100 x10^9 per L then vaginal induction
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion is indicated before procedures (aim > 50 x10^9/L for caesarean, > 80 x10^9/L for regional anaesthesia) but not to normalise counts. Transfused platelets are rapidly consumed in HELLP syndrome. The decision between vaginal delivery and caesarean depends on cervical favourability, gestational age, and urgency, not solely on platelet count. (Source: SOMANZ Guidelines)

options.text: Transfer to tertiary centre for plasma exchange as first-line HELLP treatment
options.rationale: Plasma exchange is not a standard treatment for HELLP syndrome. While it may be considered in atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome or thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura which can mimic HELLP, the clinical picture here (hypertension, proteinuria, elevated transaminases, pregnancy) is classic HELLP requiring delivery. (Source: SOMANZ Guidelines)

explanation.summary: HELLP syndrome is a severe form of pre-eclampsia characterised by haemolysis (schistocytes, elevated LDH, low haptoglobin), elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets. Definitive management is delivery. At gestational ages below 34 weeks, a short delay of 24-48 hours for antenatal corticosteroids is appropriate if the patient is stable without DIC, hepatic haematoma, eclampsia, or fetal compromise. Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM is given with a repeat dose at 24 hours. Close biochemical monitoring every 6-12 hours is essential during this window.
key_points: HELLP is definitively treated by delivery; timing depends on gestational age and stability
Corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity are prioritised at less than 34 weeks if safe to delay
Dexamethasone for HELLP reversal has not been supported by high-quality evidence
Platelet transfusion is for procedural thresholds, not for normalising counts
explanation.pearls: Class 1 HELLP (platelets < 50 x10^9/L) carries the highest complication rate including DIC (21%), placental abruption (16%), and acute renal failure (8%), and generally warrants delivery within 24 hours even at previable gestations.

stem:
A 35-year-old G2P1 woman with gestational diabetes diagnosed at 26 weeks is reviewed at 38 weeks gestation. She has been well controlled on metformin 1 g twice daily and insulin glargine 14 units at bedtime, with fasting glucose consistently 4.5-5.2 mmol/L and 2-hour postprandial levels below 6.7 mmol/L. Her most recent growth scan at 36 weeks shows an estimated fetal weight on the 72nd centile with normal amniotic fluid index and umbilical artery Doppler.

She had a previous uncomplicated vaginal delivery at term. Her cervix is 2 cm dilated, soft, and 50% effaced with the presenting part at station minus 2.

data_table.Investigations: BSL diary: fasting 4.5-5.2 mmol/L, 2-hour postprandial < 6.7 mmol/L. Growth scan 36 weeks: EFW 72nd centile, AFI 14 cm, UA Doppler normal. HbA1c at 36 weeks: 38 mmol/mol.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery recommendation?

options.text: Elective caesarean section at 39 weeks given the insulin requirement
options.rationale: Insulin requirement in GDM is not an indication for elective caesarean section. Vaginal delivery is preferred when obstetric conditions are favourable, as in this multiparous patient with a favourable cervix. Caesarean is indicated for standard obstetric reasons such as macrosomia above the 95th centile or malpresentation. (Source: ADIPS GDM Guidelines; RANZCOG)

options.text: Expectant management until spontaneous labour onset up to 41 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Allowing GDM pregnancies to continue beyond 40 weeks increases the risk of macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, and stillbirth. Australian guidelines recommend delivery by 38-39 weeks for insulin-requiring GDM. Expectant management to 41 weeks is inappropriate with insulin treatment. (Source: ADIPS GDM Guidelines)

options.text: Induction of labour between 38 and 39 weeks given her favourable cervix
options.rationale: Australian ADIPS guidelines recommend induction of labour between 38 and 39 weeks for insulin-requiring GDM with good glycaemic control and no complications. This patient has a favourable cervix (Bishop score approximately 6-7), normal fetal growth, and is multiparous, making successful induction highly likely. Earlier delivery may be considered for poor control or macrosomia. (Source: ADIPS GDM Guidelines; RANZCOG Induction of Labour Guideline)

options.text: Immediate induction today at 38 weeks due to the risk of late stillbirth
options.rationale: While the delivery window is 38-39 weeks for insulin-requiring GDM, immediate induction at exactly 38 weeks is not mandated when glycaemic control is excellent and fetal surveillance is reassuring. Induction should be planned within the 38-39 week window, not treated as an emergency. (Source: ADIPS GDM Guidelines)

options.text: Continue current management and plan delivery at 40 weeks if still undelivered
options.rationale: Delaying delivery to 40 weeks in insulin-requiring GDM exceeds the recommended 38-39 week window. Each additional week beyond 39 weeks increases the risk of macrosomia and stillbirth, particularly in insulin-treated patients. The fetal pancreas continues to respond to maternal hyperglycaemia. (Source: ADIPS GDM Guidelines)

explanation.summary: The timing of delivery in gestational diabetes depends on the level of treatment required and glycaemic control. ADIPS recommends delivery at 38-39 weeks for insulin-requiring GDM with good control, earlier if there are complications or poor control, and at 39-40 weeks for diet-controlled GDM. Induction of labour is preferred over caesarean section when obstetric conditions are favourable. Insulin should be withheld on the morning of induction and blood glucose monitored hourly during labour.
key_points: Insulin-requiring GDM with good control: deliver at 38-39 weeks
Diet-controlled GDM: deliver at 39-40 weeks
Vaginal delivery is preferred when obstetric conditions are favourable
Earlier delivery is indicated for poor glycaemic control, macrosomia, or other complications
explanation.pearls: On the day of induction for insulin-requiring GDM, the long-acting insulin (glargine or detemir) is usually given at 50% of the usual dose the night before, and the morning rapid-acting insulin and metformin are withheld, with glucose monitored hourly and an insulin-dextrose sliding scale available.

stem:
A 32-year-old G2P1 woman has a low-lying placenta identified at her 20-week morphology scan. At repeat transvaginal ultrasound at 32 weeks, the placenta has migrated and the lower edge is now 4 cm from the internal os. However, colour Doppler reveals fetal vessels traversing the membranes over the internal cervical os, consistent with a velamentous cord insertion with vasa praevia.

She is asymptomatic with no bleeding and CTG is reassuring. The fetus is in cephalic presentation with an estimated fetal weight on the 45th centile.

data_table.Investigations: TVUS 32 weeks: placental edge 4 cm from internal os, velamentous cord insertion confirmed, colour Doppler shows fetal vessels crossing internal os. EFW 45th centile. AFI 16 cm.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Induction of labour at 37 weeks with continuous CTG and amniotomy avoidance
options.rationale: Vaginal delivery is contraindicated in vasa praevia. Rupture of the fetal vessels during labour or amniotomy causes fetal haemorrhage with an extremely high mortality rate. The unprotected fetal vessels have no Wharton's jelly and rupture easily with cervical dilatation or membrane rupture. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Guideline; RCOG Green-top Guideline 27b)

options.text: Expectant management at home with weekly CTG until spontaneous labour at term
options.rationale: Outpatient management carries an unacceptable risk. Spontaneous membrane rupture or onset of labour could cause rapid fetal exsanguination before emergency caesarean can be performed. Most units recommend inpatient admission from 30-34 weeks and planned prelabour caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Guideline)

options.text: Emergency caesarean section today due to the high risk of fetal haemorrhage
options.rationale: At 32 weeks with an asymptomatic patient and reassuring CTG, emergency delivery is not indicated. The goal is to balance prematurity risks against the risk of spontaneous rupture. Planned delivery at 35-36 weeks with antenatal corticosteroids is the standard approach. Emergency CS is reserved for bleeding, labour, or membrane rupture. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Guideline)

options.text: Inpatient monitoring with corticosteroids and planned caesarean at 35-36 weeks
options.rationale: Vasa praevia diagnosed antenatally is managed with inpatient monitoring from around 30-34 weeks, antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity, and planned prelabour caesarean section at 35-36 weeks. This timing balances prematurity risk against the catastrophic risk of fetal exsanguination from vessel rupture during spontaneous labour or membrane rupture. Antenatal diagnosis reduces mortality from over 50% to approximately 3%. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Guideline; RCOG Green-top Guideline 27b)

options.text: Cervical cerclage at 32 weeks to prevent preterm labour and vessel rupture
options.rationale: Cervical cerclage is not indicated for vasa praevia. Cerclage does not protect the fetal vessels from rupture during spontaneous membrane rupture, and the procedure itself risks damaging the vessels crossing the cervical os. Management is timed delivery, not mechanical cervical support. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Guideline)

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia occurs when unprotected fetal vessels traverse the membranes over or near the internal cervical os. It is associated with velamentous cord insertion and succenturiate placental lobes.
