Salpingotomy (tube-conserving surgery) may be considered in haemodynamically stable patients when the contralateral tube is absent or damaged, but a ruptured tube rarely functions normally. This patient's history of a previous right salpingectomy means she will have no tubes after this surgery and will require IVF for future pregnancies.
key_points: Haemodynamic instability in ruptured ectopic mandates emergency laparotomy, not laparoscopy
Salpingectomy is standard for ruptured ectopic pregnancy
Methotrexate is absolutely contraindicated in haemodynamically unstable patients
A woman with bilateral salpingectomy will require IVF for future pregnancies
Ectopic pregnancy risk increases 10-fold after a previous ectopic
explanation.pearls: In haemodynamically unstable ruptured ectopic pregnancy, laparotomy allows faster peritoneal entry and haemorrhage control than laparoscopy - the mean time from skin incision to haemostasis is 5-10 minutes shorter, which can be critical in a patient with an Hb below 80 g/L.

subtopic_detail: Gestational trophoblastic disease - post-molar hCG surveillance
stem: A 25-year-old woman had an uneventful suction evacuation for a complete hydatidiform mole confirmed on histopathology 8 weeks ago. Her initial post-evacuation beta-hCG was 85,000 IU/L. Weekly beta-hCG levels have been declining steadily: 42,000, 18,000, 7,500, 3,200, 1,400, 650, 320, 280. The last two levels at weeks 7 and 8 show a plateau (320 to 280 IU/L over 3 weekly readings).

data_table.Investigations: Serial beta-hCG: Week 1: 42,000 IU/L, Week 2: 18,000, Week 3: 7,500, Week 4: 3,200, Week 5: 1,400, Week 6: 650, Week 7: 320, Week 8: 280 IU/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue weekly beta-hCG monitoring for another 4 weeks
options.rationale: A plateauing beta-hCG (less than 10% decline over 3 consecutive weekly values) after molar evacuation meets the FIGO criteria for gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. Continued observation risks disease progression and metastasis. Referral to a GTD centre for treatment is required. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease; FIGO GTN Staging)

options.text: Repeat suction evacuation of the uterus under ultrasound guidance
options.rationale: A second evacuation increases the risk of uterine perforation and Asherman syndrome and is not recommended for persistent GTN. The plateau in beta-hCG indicates persistent trophoblastic disease requiring chemotherapy, not further surgery. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease)

options.text: Oral combined contraceptive pill to suppress gonadotrophins
options.rationale: The oral contraceptive pill does not treat GTN. While reliable contraception is important during hCG surveillance (to prevent a new pregnancy confounding monitoring), the OCP does not address persistent trophoblastic disease. Contraception advice is an adjunct, not a treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease)

options.text: Hysterectomy for definitive treatment of persistent mole
options.rationale: Hysterectomy may be offered to women who have completed their family with localised disease, but is not first-line for a 25-year-old with fertility wishes. Chemotherapy is highly effective for GTN with cure rates exceeding 95% for low-risk disease. (Source: FIGO GTN Staging)

options.text: Referral to GTD centre for FIGO staging and chemotherapy
options.rationale: The plateauing beta-hCG over 3 consecutive weekly values meets FIGO criteria for gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. Referral to a specialist GTD centre (in Australia: Monash, Royal Women's, or Mater Brisbane) is required for staging investigations (CXR, pelvic ultrasound, CT if indicated) and FIGO prognostic scoring. Low-risk GTN (FIGO score 0-6) is treated with single-agent methotrexate with cure rates exceeding 95%. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease; FIGO GTN Staging)

explanation.summary: Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN) is diagnosed after molar evacuation when beta-hCG plateaus (less than 10% decline over 3 consecutive weekly values), rises over 2 consecutive weeks, remains detectable for more than 6 months, or histologically confirmed choriocarcinoma or PSTT is present. Australia has three specialised GTD centres. FIGO scoring combines age, antecedent pregnancy, interval, pre-treatment hCG, tumour size, metastatic sites, number of metastases, and prior failed chemotherapy to stratify risk. Low-risk GTN is cured in over 95% of cases with single-agent methotrexate.
key_points: GTN diagnosis: beta-hCG plateau (less than 10% decline over 3 weekly values), rise over 2 weeks, or persistence beyond 6 months
Referral to a specialist GTD centre is mandatory for FIGO staging and treatment
Low-risk GTN (FIGO score 0-6) is treated with single-agent methotrexate with over 95% cure rate
Reliable contraception is required during hCG surveillance to prevent confounding by a new pregnancy
Post-treatment hCG surveillance continues for 12 months after normalisation for complete mole
explanation.pearls: After complete molar evacuation, the FIGO criterion for GTN diagnosis is a beta-hCG plateau of less than 10% decline across 3 consecutive weekly measurements - this triggers referral to a GTD centre, not continued observation.

stem: A 32-year-old woman at 34 weeks gestation collapses in the hospital corridor. She is found to be pulseless and apnoeic. The cardiac arrest team begins CPR. The uterine fundus is palpable above the umbilicus. After 4 minutes of high-quality CPR with adrenaline administered, there is no return of spontaneous circulation.

data_table.Vital signs: Cardiac arrest. No pulse. No spontaneous breathing. Uterine fundus palpable 4 cm above the umbilicus (consistent with approximately 34 weeks).

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue CPR for a further 10 minutes before considering surgery
options.rationale: Delaying perimortem caesarean section beyond 5 minutes of cardiac arrest reduces both maternal and fetal survival. The gravid uterus above 20 weeks compresses the inferior vena cava and aorta, reducing venous return and cardiac output during CPR by up to 30%. Delivery of the fetus and placenta improves maternal haemodynamics. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline: Cardiac Arrest in Pregnancy; RANZCOG: Maternal Collapse)
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline: Cardiac Arrest in Pregnancy

options.text: Left lateral tilt and continue CPR until ROSC is achieved
options.rationale: Left lateral tilt (or manual left uterine displacement) should be applied from the start of CPR but is a temporising measure. If ROSC is not achieved within 4-5 minutes, perimortem caesarean section must be performed. CPR effectiveness is significantly impaired by aortocaval compression even with optimal tilt. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline: Cardiac Arrest in Pregnancy)
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline: Cardiac Arrest in Pregnancy

options.text: Transfer to theatre for caesarean section under sterile conditions
options.rationale: Perimortem caesarean section should be performed at the point of arrest - do not move the patient to theatre. Transfer wastes critical minutes and interrupts CPR. The procedure is performed with whatever equipment is available, prioritising speed. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline: Cardiac Arrest in Pregnancy)
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline: Cardiac Arrest in Pregnancy

options.text: Perimortem caesarean section performed at the point of arrest
options.rationale: Perimortem caesarean section should be commenced by 4 minutes and the baby delivered by 5 minutes of maternal cardiac arrest when ROSC has not been achieved. The primary purpose is to improve maternal resuscitation by relieving aortocaval compression. Fetal survival is a secondary benefit. The procedure is performed at the point of arrest with a vertical midline incision, without waiting for sterile conditions or an operating theatre. CPR continues throughout. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline: Cardiac Arrest in Pregnancy; RANZCOG: Maternal Collapse)
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline: Cardiac Arrest in Pregnancy

options.text: Bedside ultrasound to confirm fetal viability before proceeding
options.rationale: Ultrasound to check fetal viability should not delay perimortem caesarean section. The primary indication for the procedure is maternal resuscitation (relief of aortocaval compression), not fetal delivery. Even if the fetus is already dead, removing the gravid uterus improves maternal cardiac output during CPR. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline: Cardiac Arrest in Pregnancy)
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline: Cardiac Arrest in Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Perimortem caesarean section is performed during maternal cardiac arrest when ROSC has not been achieved within 4-5 minutes and the uterine fundus is at or above the umbilicus (approximately 20 weeks). The primary purpose is maternal - relieving aortocaval compression improves venous return and cardiac output during CPR by up to 30%. The decision to perform the procedure should be made by 4 minutes, with delivery by 5 minutes. The procedure is performed at the point of arrest, not in an operating theatre. CPR continues throughout and after delivery.
key_points: Perimortem caesarean section decision by 4 minutes, delivery by 5 minutes of maternal cardiac arrest
Primary indication is maternal resuscitation, not fetal delivery
Perform at the point of arrest - do not transfer to theatre
Aortocaval compression reduces cardiac output by up to 30% in the supine gravid patient after 20 weeks
CPR must continue during and after the procedure - ROSC may occur after delivery
explanation.pearls: Perimortem caesarean section is a MATERNAL resuscitation procedure, not a fetal rescue operation - even when the fetus is known to be dead, removing the gravid uterus after 20 weeks improves venous return and may achieve ROSC where CPR alone failed.

sources.label: ANZCOR Guideline: Cardiac Arrest in Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Ovarian cyst in pregnancy - management by trimester
stem: A 29-year-old woman at 14 weeks gestation is found to have a 7 cm simple unilocular ovarian cyst on her dating scan. She is asymptomatic with no pain, nausea, or fever. A repeat ultrasound at 14 weeks confirms the cyst is persistent, simple (anechoic, thin-walled, no solid components, no internal septations), measuring 7.2 cm on the left ovary. CA-125 is 45 U/mL.

data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound 8 weeks: 6.8 cm simple left ovarian cyst. Ultrasound 14 weeks: 7.2 cm simple left ovarian cyst, unchanged morphology. No ascites. CA-125: 45 U/mL (note: CA-125 is physiologically elevated in pregnancy, especially first trimester).

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Urgent laparotomy for ovarian cyst removal this week
options.rationale: Urgent surgical intervention is not indicated for an asymptomatic simple cyst without concerning features. Laparotomy carries higher morbidity than laparoscopy and is not the preferred approach for benign-appearing cysts. Surgery, if required, can be performed electively. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian Masses in Pregnancy; RCOG Green-top Guideline: Adnexal Masses)

options.text: Observation with repeat ultrasound at 18-20 weeks
options.rationale: Observation is reasonable for small simple cysts, but a persistent simple cyst of 7 cm or larger has a higher risk of torsion, rupture, or obstruction during pregnancy and labour. At 14 weeks (early second trimester), the optimal surgical window is now, as the miscarriage risk from surgery is lowest between 14-18 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian Masses in Pregnancy)

options.text: Laparoscopic cystectomy between 14 and 18 weeks gestation
options.rationale: A persistent simple ovarian cyst of 7 cm or larger in pregnancy warrants surgical consideration due to the risk of torsion (10-15% for cysts above 5 cm), rupture, and obstructed labour. The optimal window for elective surgery in pregnancy is 14-18 weeks - after organogenesis is complete (reducing teratogenic risk from anaesthesia) and before the uterus is too large for laparoscopic access. Laparoscopy is preferred over laparotomy for benign-appearing cysts. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian Masses in Pregnancy; RCOG Green-top Guideline: Adnexal Masses)

options.text: CT pelvis to better characterise the cyst before deciding
options.rationale: CT pelvis involves ionising radiation and should be avoided in pregnancy unless absolutely necessary. MRI without gadolinium is the preferred cross-sectional imaging modality in pregnancy if further characterisation is needed beyond ultrasound. However, this cyst is simple and well-characterised on ultrasound. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian Masses in Pregnancy)

options.text: Ultrasound-guided aspiration of the cyst contents
options.rationale: Aspiration of ovarian cysts has a high recurrence rate (up to 70%) and does not provide histological diagnosis. It is not recommended as definitive management. Surgical excision (cystectomy) is preferred for persistent large cysts requiring intervention. (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline: Adnexal Masses)

explanation.summary: Adnexal masses are found in 1-2% of pregnancies, most commonly corpus luteum cysts that resolve by 16 weeks. Persistent cysts above 5-6 cm carry a significant risk of torsion (10-15%), and those above 7 cm are at additional risk of obstructing labour. The optimal surgical window in pregnancy is 14-18 weeks gestation, after organogenesis and before the uterus limits laparoscopic access. Simple cysts with benign ultrasound features can be managed with laparoscopic cystectomy. CA-125 is unreliable in pregnancy as it is physiologically elevated in the first trimester.
key_points: Persistent ovarian cysts above 5-6 cm in pregnancy carry a 10-15% risk of torsion
Optimal surgical window in pregnancy is 14-18 weeks gestation
Laparoscopy is safe in pregnancy and preferred over laparotomy for benign-appearing cysts
CA-125 is physiologically elevated in pregnancy and unreliable for malignancy risk assessment
MRI without gadolinium is the preferred cross-sectional imaging if ultrasound is insufficient
explanation.pearls: CA-125 levels are physiologically elevated in the first trimester of pregnancy (up to 100 U/mL or higher) due to decidual production - a mildly elevated CA-125 in early pregnancy should not raise concern for malignancy in the context of a simple-appearing ovarian cyst.

subtopic_detail: Fibroids in pregnancy - red degeneration management
stem: A 33-year-old woman at 22 weeks gestation presents with acute onset right-sided abdominal pain, nausea, and low-grade fever. She has a known 8 cm intramural uterine fibroid documented on her dating scan. The pain is localised to the right flank and is constant. She has no vaginal bleeding or contractions.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 98, BP 120/75 mmHg, Temp 37.8 C, RR 18
data_table.Examination: Localised tenderness over the right lateral aspect of the uterus corresponding to the known fibroid location. The fibroid is exquisitely tender on palpation. No peritoneal signs. Cervix closed and long on digital examination.
data_table.Investigations: WCC 13.2 x10^9/L, CRP 42 mg/L. Urinalysis: no leucocytes, no nitrites. Ultrasound: 8.5 cm intramural fibroid with heterogeneous echotexture suggesting internal haemorrhage. Fetus viable, normal amniotic fluid.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Analgesia, hydration, and supportive care with monitoring
options.rationale: Red (carneous) degeneration of a fibroid in pregnancy is caused by haemorrhagic infarction of the fibroid due to outgrowing its blood supply. Management is conservative: rest, hydration, and analgesia (paracetamol as first-line, short courses of NSAIDs may be used cautiously before 30 weeks). The pain typically resolves within 7-14 days. Surgical intervention (myomectomy) in pregnancy carries high risks of haemorrhage and preterm labour and is reserved for failure of medical management. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in Pregnancy; eTG: Obstetric)

options.text: Urgent myomectomy to remove the degenerating fibroid
options.rationale: Myomectomy during pregnancy carries a very high risk of uncontrollable haemorrhage due to the increased uterine vascularity. It also increases the risk of preterm labour and emergency hysterectomy. Surgery is reserved for rare complications such as torsion of a pedunculated fibroid or refractory pain not responding to 2-3 weeks of conservative management. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in Pregnancy)

options.text: IV antibiotics for suspected infected fibroid or abscess
options.rationale: Infected fibroids are extremely rare. The mild leucocytosis and low-grade fever in this context are consistent with the inflammatory response of red degeneration, not infection. There is no indication for antibiotics. The ultrasound shows internal haemorrhage consistent with degeneration, not an abscess collection. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in Pregnancy)

options.text: Uterine artery embolisation to infarct the fibroid
options.rationale: Uterine artery embolisation is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy as it risks placental infarction, fetal death, and uterine necrosis. It is used for symptomatic fibroids in non-pregnant women who wish to avoid surgery. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in Pregnancy)

options.text: Delivery by caesarean section to relieve the complication
options.rationale: At 22 weeks gestation the fetus is at the lower limit of viability and delivery would result in extreme prematurity with very high morbidity and mortality. Red degeneration is a self-limiting condition that resolves with conservative management. Delivery is not indicated. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Red (carneous) degeneration of a uterine fibroid typically occurs in the second and early third trimester when the rapidly growing fibroid outstrips its blood supply, causing haemorrhagic infarction. The classic presentation is acute localised uterine pain over the fibroid, low-grade fever, and mild leucocytosis. Ultrasound may show heterogeneous echotexture within the fibroid. Management is conservative with rest, hydration, and analgesia. The condition is self-limiting over 7-14 days. Surgical intervention is reserved for rare complications and carries significant risks during pregnancy.
key_points: Red degeneration occurs in the second trimester when the fibroid outgrows its blood supply
Conservative management (analgesia, hydration, rest) is first-line with resolution in 7-14 days
Myomectomy in pregnancy carries very high haemorrhage risk and is reserved for refractory cases
Low-grade fever and leucocytosis are expected features of the inflammatory response, not infection
Uterine artery embolisation is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy
explanation.pearls: Paracetamol is first-line analgesia for red degeneration in pregnancy, but short courses of indometacin (48-72 hours) may be used before 30 weeks if paracetamol is insufficient - after 30 weeks, NSAIDs risk premature ductal closure and should be avoided.

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents to the early pregnancy assessment unit at 7 weeks gestation with mild left iliac fossa pain and light vaginal bleeding. She is haemodynamically stable. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 22 mm left adnexal mass with a yolk sac but no cardiac activity, and an empty uterus. There is a small amount of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. She has no significant past medical history, normal renal and hepatic function, and no history of methotrexate allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 118/72 mmHg, Temp 36.8
data_table.Investigations: beta-hCG 4,200 IU/L; FBC: Hb 128 g/L, WCC 7.8, platelets 245; LFTs and UEC normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Expectant management with serial beta-hCG monitoring
options.rationale: Expectant management may be considered for tubal ectopics with beta-hCG below 1,500 IU/L and declining levels. With a beta-hCG of 4,200 IU/L and a visible adnexal mass with yolk sac, the ectopic is too advanced for safe expectant management due to increased rupture risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Ectopic Pregnancy)

options.text: Administer single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2
options.rationale: Methotrexate is used for selected unruptured ectopic pregnancies but has specific eligibility criteria. The presence of a yolk sac within the ectopic and a beta-hCG above 4,000 IU/L are relative contraindications - RANZCOG guidelines suggest methotrexate is most effective when beta-hCG is below 5,000, but the visible yolk sac and size of 22 mm significantly increase failure risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Ectopic Pregnancy)

options.text: Repeat the beta-hCG in 48 hours to assess the trajectory
options.rationale: Repeating beta-hCG is useful when the diagnosis is uncertain (pregnancy of unknown location). Here the diagnosis is confirmed - an ectopic pregnancy with a visible adnexal mass containing a yolk sac. Delaying definitive management to await a repeat level risks tubal rupture with this beta-hCG level and ectopic size. (Source: RANZCOG: Ectopic Pregnancy)

options.text: Proceed with laparoscopic salpingostomy or salpingectomy
options.rationale: Surgical management is the most appropriate option for this ectopic pregnancy. The combination of a 22 mm adnexal mass with a visible yolk sac and beta-hCG of 4,200 IU/L indicates a relatively advanced ectopic pregnancy where methotrexate failure risk is high. Laparoscopic surgery allows definitive treatment. Salpingectomy is preferred unless the contralateral tube is damaged or absent. (Source: RANZCOG: Ectopic Pregnancy)

options.text: Administer anti-D immunoglobulin and reassess in one week
options.rationale: Anti-D immunoglobulin should be given to Rh-negative women with ectopic pregnancy, but the question does not state she is Rh-negative. Regardless, anti-D is an adjunct, not a management strategy for the ectopic itself. Reassessing in one week without definitive treatment risks tubal rupture. (Source: RANZCOG: Ectopic Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Ectopic pregnancy management depends on clinical stability, beta-hCG level, ultrasound features, and patient preference. Methotrexate is suitable for selected small, unruptured ectopics with beta-hCG typically below 5,000 IU/L and no cardiac activity or yolk sac. When these criteria are not met, surgical management via laparoscopy is preferred. Salpingectomy is the standard approach unless there are fertility-preserving indications for salpingostomy. All Rh-negative women should receive anti-D.
key_points: Methotrexate eligibility requires no cardiac activity, ideally no yolk sac, and beta-hCG below 5,000 IU/L
Visible yolk sac and ectopic size above 35 mm are relative contraindications to methotrexate
Laparoscopic salpingectomy is the standard surgical approach for tubal ectopics
Expectant management is only for beta-hCG below 1,500 IU/L with declining trend
Salpingostomy may be considered when the contralateral tube is damaged or absent
explanation.pearls: The presence of cardiac activity within an ectopic pregnancy is an absolute contraindication to methotrexate - these patients require surgical management regardless of beta-hCG level.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid syndrome is reviewed in the gynaecology clinic. She takes warfarin for a previous deep vein thrombosis and hydroxychloroquine for her SLE. She had a miscarriage at 14 weeks gestation six months ago and does not wish to become pregnant for at least three years. Her periods are regular and she is normotensive. She asks about the most effective reversible contraception that is safe for her.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74 mmHg, BMI 24
data_table.Investigations: INR 2.4 (target 2.0-3.0); recent FBC, UEC, LFTs all normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraceptive recommendation?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill containing low-dose oestrogen
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraceptives (pill, patch, ring) are absolutely contraindicated in women with antiphospholipid syndrome or a history of VTE, as oestrogen increases thrombotic risk. This is a Category 4 (unacceptable health risk) in the WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria and the Australian adaptation. (Source: FSRH: Medical Eligibility Criteria)

options.text: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate injection every 12 weeks
options.rationale: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate is a progestogen-only method and avoids oestrogen-related thrombotic risk. However, it is Category 3 (risks generally outweigh benefits) in women with current VTE on anticoagulation due to uncertain effects on coagulation and bone density concerns with long-term use. The levonorgestrel IUD offers superior efficacy and a better safety profile. (Source: FSRH: Medical Eligibility Criteria)

options.text: Levonorgestrel intrauterine device for long-acting protection
options.rationale: The levonorgestrel IUD is Category 1 (no restriction) for women with a history of VTE or current anticoagulation. It provides highly effective long-acting reversible contraception with minimal systemic hormonal absorption. It may also reduce menstrual blood loss, which is beneficial in a woman on warfarin who may experience heavy menstrual bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG: Contraception)

options.text: Etonogestrel subdermal implant inserted in the non-dominant arm
options.rationale: The etonogestrel implant is a progestogen-only method and is Category 2 (benefits generally outweigh risks) for women with VTE history. It is a reasonable option, but the levonorgestrel IUD is preferred in this scenario because it has even less systemic hormonal absorption and offers additional benefit of reducing menstrual bleeding in a woman on anticoagulation. (Source: FSRH: Medical Eligibility Criteria)

options.text: Copper intrauterine device for non-hormonal long-acting effect
options.rationale: The copper IUD provides effective non-hormonal contraception. However, it typically increases menstrual blood loss by 20-50%, which is problematic for a woman on therapeutic anticoagulation with warfarin. The levonorgestrel IUD is preferable as it reduces menstrual bleeding while providing equivalent contraceptive efficacy. (Source: RANZCOG: Contraception)

explanation.summary: Contraceptive choice in women with antiphospholipid syndrome and VTE history requires avoidance of oestrogen-containing methods due to thrombotic risk. The levonorgestrel IUD is the optimal choice as it is highly effective, has minimal systemic absorption, is Category 1 for VTE, and reduces menstrual blood loss - a significant advantage for women on anticoagulation. The copper IUD, while non-hormonal, increases menstrual bleeding and is less suitable for anticoagulated women.
key_points: Combined hormonal contraceptives are Category 4 (absolutely contraindicated) in antiphospholipid syndrome and VTE history
Levonorgestrel IUD is Category 1 (no restriction) and reduces menstrual bleeding
Copper IUD increases menstrual loss by 20-50% and is problematic with anticoagulation
The etonogestrel implant is acceptable but has more systemic hormonal absorption than the levonorgestrel IUD
Depot medroxyprogesterone is Category 3 in current VTE on anticoagulation
explanation.pearls: The levonorgestrel IUD achieves endometrial progestogen concentrations 1000 times higher than systemic levels, providing excellent contraception and menstrual control while maintaining a Category 1 safety rating even in women with VTE on anticoagulation.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset right iliac fossa pain that woke her from sleep 4 hours ago. She reports two episodes of vomiting. Her last menstrual period was 12 days ago and she has a known 6 cm right ovarian dermoid cyst found incidentally on ultrasound 3 months ago. She has no vaginal bleeding or discharge. On examination she has right iliac fossa tenderness with guarding but no rebound. Bowel sounds are present.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102, BP 122/78 mmHg, Temp 37.1, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta-hCG: negative; FBC: WCC 12.4 x10^9/L; CRP 18 mg/L; urinalysis: normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Arrange CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast urgently
options.rationale: CT may demonstrate an enlarged ovary with reduced enhancement, but it is not the first-line investigation for suspected ovarian torsion in a young woman. Pelvic ultrasound with Doppler is the preferred initial imaging modality - it avoids radiation, can visualise the cyst, and assess ovarian blood flow. CT is reserved for equivocal cases or when alternative diagnoses are considered. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Gynaecology)

options.text: Administer analgesia and commence a trial of oral antibiotics
options.rationale: This presentation is not consistent with a pelvic infection - there is no fever, no vaginal discharge, and the negative urine pregnancy test makes PID with ectopic less likely. The sudden onset, vomiting, and known ovarian cyst are classic for torsion. Antibiotics would delay diagnosis and definitive management. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Gynaecology)

options.text: Observe with serial abdominal examinations over six hours
options.rationale: Ovarian torsion is a time-critical diagnosis - prolonged ischaemia leads to irreversible ovarian damage. Observation alone delays diagnosis and risks loss of the ovary. The combination of sudden-onset pain, vomiting, and a known ovarian mass should prompt urgent investigation and consideration of surgical exploration. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Ovarian Torsion)

options.text: Request urgent pelvic ultrasound with Doppler flow assessment
options.rationale: Pelvic ultrasound with Doppler is the first-line investigation for suspected ovarian torsion. It can demonstrate the enlarged ovary, the dermoid cyst, and assess arterial and venous flow. However, normal Doppler flow does not exclude torsion (sensitivity approximately 60-70% for absent flow) as intermittent torsion may allow transient reperfusion. If clinical suspicion remains high despite normal Doppler, diagnostic laparoscopy should proceed. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Gynaecology)

options.text: Proceed directly to diagnostic laparoscopy without imaging
options.rationale: Diagnostic laparoscopy is the definitive investigation and treatment for ovarian torsion, and proceeding directly may be appropriate if the diagnosis is near-certain and imaging would cause delay. However, ultrasound is rapid, non-invasive, and may reveal alternative diagnoses (ruptured cyst, ectopic pregnancy) that change management. It should be attempted first unless the patient is haemodynamically unstable. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Gynaecology)

explanation.summary: Ovarian torsion occurs when the ovary rotates on its vascular pedicle, compromising blood flow. It is more common with ovarian masses above 5 cm, with dermoid cysts being the most common associated pathology. The classic presentation is sudden-onset unilateral pelvic pain with vomiting. Pelvic ultrasound with Doppler is the first-line investigation, but normal Doppler does not exclude torsion due to intermittent twisting. If clinical suspicion remains high, diagnostic laparoscopy should proceed regardless of imaging findings.
key_points: Ovarian masses above 5 cm increase torsion risk, with dermoid cysts being the most common association
Pelvic ultrasound with Doppler is first-line but has limited sensitivity for torsion (normal flow does not exclude it)
Ovarian torsion is a surgical emergency - prolonged ischaemia leads to irreversible damage
Detorsion with ovarian conservation is preferred over oophorectomy, especially in young women
The classic triad is sudden-onset unilateral pelvic pain, vomiting, and a known or palpable adnexal mass
explanation.pearls: Normal Doppler flow on ultrasound does NOT exclude ovarian torsion - the ovary may intermittently detort and re-tort, transiently restoring flow; if clinical suspicion is high, proceed to laparoscopy regardless.

stem: A 28-year-old woman in her second pregnancy is reviewed at 20 weeks gestation. Her first pregnancy ended in a spontaneous second-trimester loss at 18 weeks with painless cervical dilatation. Her current pregnancy has been uncomplicated so far. A transvaginal ultrasound at her morphology scan shows a cervical length of 18 mm with funnelling of the internal os. She has no contractions, no vaginal bleeding, and the membranes are intact. The fetus has normal anatomy on ultrasound.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 112/68 mmHg, HR 78, Temp 36.7
data_table.Investigations: Cervical length 18 mm with funnelling; fetal anatomy normal; amniotic fluid index normal; group B streptococcus status unknown

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence vaginal progesterone 200 mg nightly as monotherapy
options.rationale: Vaginal progesterone is effective for preventing preterm birth in women with a short cervix found incidentally on ultrasound without a history of cervical insufficiency. However, this woman has a classical history of cervical insufficiency (previous painless second-trimester loss) with a short cervix and funnelling. She is a candidate for cerclage, which provides superior outcomes in this specific high-risk population. (Source: RANZCOG: Cervical Insufficiency)

options.text: Bed rest and weekly cervical length surveillance by ultrasound
options.rationale: Bed rest has not been shown to prevent preterm birth or cervical shortening in any randomised trial and is no longer recommended. Serial cervical length monitoring alone does not treat the underlying cervical insufficiency. Active intervention is warranted given the history and ultrasound findings. (Source: RANZCOG: Cervical Insufficiency)

options.text: Commence tocolytic therapy with nifedipine to prevent contractions
options.rationale: Tocolytic therapy is used for acute preterm labour with contractions to buy time for corticosteroid administration. This woman has no contractions - her cervical changes are due to cervical insufficiency, not preterm labour. Tocolytics do not treat cervical incompetence and would not prevent further dilatation. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm Labour)

options.text: Insert a cervical cerclage and commence vaginal progesterone
options.rationale: Cervical cerclage is the correct intervention for cervical insufficiency with a compatible history and short cervix. However, in current practice for history-indicated cerclage, the optimal timing is 12-14 weeks gestation. At 20 weeks with a cervix of 18 mm and funnelling, this is now a rescue cerclage, and adding vaginal progesterone to cerclage has not been shown to provide additional benefit in women already receiving cerclage. (Source: RANZCOG: Cervical Insufficiency)

options.text: Insert an emergency rescue cerclage after excluding infection
options.rationale: This woman has a classic history of cervical insufficiency (previous painless mid-trimester loss) and now has a short cervix at 18 mm with funnelling at 20 weeks. This presentation warrants rescue cerclage. Before insertion, subclinical infection must be excluded with amniocentesis or vaginal swabs, as cerclage in the presence of infection increases the risk of complications. The window for cerclage typically closes at 24 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: Cervical Insufficiency)

explanation.summary: Cervical insufficiency is characterised by painless cervical dilatation leading to second-trimester pregnancy loss. Management depends on the clinical scenario. History-indicated cerclage is placed at 12-14 weeks in women with a classic history. Ultrasound-indicated cerclage is placed when a short cervix (typically <25 mm) is detected in a woman with a prior preterm birth or mid-trimester loss. Rescue cerclage is performed when cervical changes are advanced (dilatation with or without membrane prolapse). Infection must be excluded before rescue cerclage.
key_points: History-indicated cerclage is ideally placed at 12-14 weeks gestation
Rescue cerclage at 20 weeks requires exclusion of subclinical infection before insertion
Vaginal progesterone is first-line for incidental short cervix without a history of cervical insufficiency
Bed rest has no proven benefit for cervical insufficiency or preterm birth prevention
The window for cerclage generally closes at 24 weeks gestation
explanation.pearls: The distinction between history-indicated (12-14 weeks), ultrasound-indicated (<25 mm cervix in high-risk woman), and rescue cerclage (advanced changes with membranes visible) determines both timing and pre-operative requirements - rescue cerclage mandates amniocentesis or vaginal cultures to exclude infection.

stem: A 34-year-old multiparous woman at 39 weeks gestation is in active labour with artificial rupture of membranes performed 20 minutes ago. She suddenly becomes agitated and dyspnoeic, then loses consciousness. Within minutes she develops tonic-clonic seizure activity. After initial resuscitation and seizure termination with midazolam, she is intubated. An emergency caesarean section is performed. Post-delivery, she develops profuse uterine bleeding that does not respond to uterotonics. Blood is noted to be non-clotting from IV sites and surgical wound.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 135, BP 72/40 mmHg, SpO2 88% on FiO2 1.0, Temp 36.2
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.08, lactate 8.4 mmol/L; FBC: Hb 68 g/L, platelets 32 x10^9/L; coags: PT 28 sec, APTT 62 sec, fibrinogen 0.4 g/L; D-dimer >20,000 ng/mL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management priority?

options.text: Activate the massive transfusion protocol and give cryoprecipitate
options.rationale: This presentation is consistent with amniotic fluid embolism (AFE) complicated by disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and haemorrhagic shock. The immediate priority is addressing the coagulopathy and haemorrhage through massive transfusion protocol activation. Cryoprecipitate is critical to replace fibrinogen (target >2 g/L in obstetric haemorrhage). Packed red cells, fresh frozen plasma, and platelets should be given concurrently in a ratio-based approach. (Source: RANZCOG: PPH; NBA: Massive Transfusion)

options.text: Administer IV heparin infusion to treat the underlying DIC
options.rationale: Heparin is sometimes used in chronic compensated DIC but is contraindicated in acute consumptive DIC with active haemorrhage. Giving heparin to a patient with fibrinogen of 0.4 g/L and profuse bleeding would worsen the haemorrhage catastrophically. The treatment for acute DIC with bleeding is replacement of consumed clotting factors. (Source: RANZCOG: PPH)

options.text: Commence IV magnesium sulfate for presumed eclamptic seizures
options.rationale: Eclampsia should be considered in any pregnant woman with seizures. However, the clinical picture here - sudden cardiovascular collapse with hypoxia immediately after membrane rupture, followed by DIC with non-clotting blood - is characteristic of AFE, not eclampsia. Eclampsia does not typically cause DIC or refractory haemorrhage. Treatment of the coagulopathy is the priority. (Source: RANZCOG: PPH)

options.text: Perform perimortem hysterectomy to control uterine haemorrhage
options.rationale: Hysterectomy may ultimately be necessary if haemorrhage cannot be controlled, but it should not be the first intervention. The coagulopathy must be corrected first - operating on a patient with fibrinogen 0.4 g/L and platelets of 32 will result in uncontrollable surgical bleeding. Massive transfusion and coagulation factor replacement take priority. (Source: NBA: Massive Transfusion)

options.text: Administer IV tranexamic acid 1 g and repeat uterotonics only
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid is an important adjunct in obstetric haemorrhage and should be given. However, uterotonics have already failed and the fundamental problem is DIC with consumed clotting factors. Tranexamic acid alone cannot replace fibrinogen or clotting factors. The priority is massive transfusion protocol with cryoprecipitate to restore haemostasis. (Source: RANZCOG: PPH)

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare but catastrophic obstetric emergency with a mortality rate of 20-60%. It classically presents with sudden cardiovascular collapse, hypoxia, and seizures during labour or immediately postpartum, followed by DIC and haemorrhage. The pathophysiology involves an abnormal maternal immune response to fetal material entering the circulation. Management is supportive - there is no specific treatment. The immediate priority is haemodynamic resuscitation and correction of coagulopathy through massive transfusion.
key_points: AFE classically presents with sudden cardiovascular collapse, hypoxia, seizures, and DIC
DIC in AFE is consumptive - treat with replacement of clotting factors, not heparin
Fibrinogen target in obstetric haemorrhage is above 2 g/L - cryoprecipitate is the fastest way to replace it
Massive transfusion protocol should be activated early with ratio-based product administration
Hysterectomy may be needed but only after coagulopathy correction - surgical haemostasis requires functional clotting
explanation.pearls: In obstetric DIC from AFE, fibrinogen falls earlier and more precipitously than in non-obstetric DIC because baseline fibrinogen in pregnancy is already elevated (4-6 g/L) - a level that appears 'normal' at 2 g/L actually represents a 50% drop and warrants urgent cryoprecipitate.

stem: A 35-year-old woman in her fourth pregnancy is found to have an anterior low-lying placenta at her 20-week morphology scan. She has had two previous caesarean sections and one vaginal delivery. She is asymptomatic with no vaginal bleeding. The sonographer notes lacunae within the placental substance and loss of the normal retroplacental clear zone on ultrasound. The woman asks about the implications of these findings.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 76
data_table.Investigations: Morphology scan: anterior low-lying placenta covering internal os, multiple placental lacunae, loss of retroplacental clear zone, bladder wall irregularity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Reassure that the placenta will likely migrate and rescan at 32 weeks
options.rationale: While placental migration does occur (up to 90% of low-lying placentas at 20 weeks will resolve), the ultrasound features described - lacunae, loss of retroplacental clear zone, and bladder wall irregularity - are highly suggestive of placenta accreta spectrum. This changes the management from expectant to planned multidisciplinary delivery. Reassurance alone is inappropriate. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta Accreta Spectrum)

options.text: Refer to a tertiary centre for MRI and multidisciplinary planning
options.rationale: The combination of previous caesarean sections, anterior placenta praevia, and ultrasound features of accreta (lacunae, loss of clear zone, bladder involvement) constitutes suspected placenta accreta spectrum. Management requires referral to a tertiary centre with interventional radiology, urology, and experienced obstetric surgical teams. MRI can further characterise the depth of invasion. Planned delivery is typically at 35-36 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta Accreta Spectrum)

options.text: Schedule elective caesarean section at 39 weeks at the local hospital
options.rationale: Waiting until 39 weeks risks emergency presentation with life-threatening haemorrhage in suspected placenta accreta spectrum. Guidelines recommend planned delivery at 35-36 weeks at a tertiary centre with multidisciplinary surgical capability. Delivery at a local hospital without appropriate resources risks maternal death from uncontrollable haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta Accreta Spectrum)

options.text: Commence low-dose aspirin to prevent placental insufficiency
options.rationale: Low-dose aspirin is used for pre-eclampsia prevention in high-risk women but has no role in managing placenta accreta spectrum. The abnormal placentation is already established by 20 weeks and aspirin cannot alter the depth of placental invasion. Aspirin may also theoretically increase bleeding risk in a condition already associated with massive haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta Accreta Spectrum)

options.text: Arrange serial ultrasounds every 2 weeks to monitor invasion depth
options.rationale: Serial ultrasound monitoring is part of the follow-up plan but is not the most appropriate management in isolation. The finding of suspected placenta accreta spectrum in a woman with multiple prior caesareans requires immediate referral to a tertiary centre for comprehensive planning, not just surveillance at the local facility. The invasion depth does not change the need for tertiary referral. (Source: FIGO: Placenta Accreta Spectrum)

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum describes abnormal placental adherence to the myometrium, ranging from accreta (superficial) through increta (into myometrium) to percreta (through myometrium to adjacent organs). The major risk factor is placenta praevia overlying a previous caesarean scar. Ultrasound features include placental lacunae, loss of the retroplacental clear zone, and bladder wall involvement. Management requires multidisciplinary planning at a tertiary centre with planned caesarean hysterectomy typically at 35-36 weeks.
key_points: Placenta praevia overlying previous caesarean scar significantly increases accreta risk (up to 60% with 3 prior sections)
Ultrasound features: lacunae, loss of retroplacental clear zone, bladder wall irregularity, bridging vessels
MRI adds value for assessing depth of myometrial invasion and parametrial involvement
Delivery is typically planned at 35-36 weeks at a tertiary centre with multidisciplinary team
Caesarean hysterectomy is often required - attempting placental removal risks life-threatening haemorrhage
explanation.pearls: The risk of placenta accreta spectrum increases exponentially with the number of prior caesarean sections - 3% after one, 11% after two, 40% after three, and 67% after four or more when combined with placenta praevia.

stem: A 29-year-old primigravida is referred at 28 weeks gestation after her fundal height measures 3 cm below expected. She has no significant medical history and is a non-smoker. Transvaginal ultrasound confirms a structurally normal fetus. Serology screening for infection is negative and karyotype is normal.

data_table.Ultrasound findings: Estimated fetal weight: Below 3rd centile for gestation; Abdominal circumference: Below 3rd centile for gestation; Umbilical artery Doppler: Absent end-diastolic flow; Middle cerebral artery Doppler: Reduced pulsatility index (brain-sparing); Ductus venosus Doppler: Normal a-wave; Amniotic fluid index: 6 cm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Administer antenatal corticosteroids and plan delivery within 48 hours following multidisciplinary discussion at a tertiary centre
options.rationale: At 28 weeks with absent end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery and evidence of brain-sparing on MCA Doppler, this fetus has significant placental insufficiency. Although the ductus venosus remains normal, the combination of absent end-diastolic flow and brain-sparing indicates a high risk of fetal compromise. Antenatal corticosteroids should be administered for fetal lung maturation and delivery planned within 48 hours at a tertiary centre with appropriate neonatal intensive care. The TRUFFLE study and RANZCOG guidelines support delivery at this gestation when umbilical artery Doppler shows absent end-diastolic flow with evidence of fetal redistribution. (Source: RANZCOG FGR guideline)

options.text: Continue twice-weekly Doppler surveillance and cardiotocography with plan for delivery only if ductus venosus a-wave becomes reversed
options.rationale: Waiting for ductus venosus abnormality before delivery would be inappropriate given absent end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery with brain-sparing already present. While ductus venosus Doppler is used to guide timing in early-onset FGR, delaying delivery until the a-wave reverses risks fetal death. Current evidence from the TRUFFLE study supports delivery when multiple parameters of deterioration are present, not waiting for a single late-stage finding in isolation. (Source: RANZCOG FGR guideline)

options.text: Reassure the patient that this likely represents a constitutionally small fetus and repeat growth ultrasound in two weeks with standard antenatal care
options.rationale: This is not a constitutionally small fetus. The abnormal umbilical artery Doppler with absent end-diastolic flow and MCA brain-sparing pattern clearly indicate placental insufficiency. A constitutionally small fetus would have normal Doppler studies and symmetrical smallness consistent with parental phenotype. Delaying intervention for two weeks in this clinical scenario risks intrauterine fetal death. (Source: ISUOG FGR guideline)

options.text: Start low-dose aspirin 150 mg daily and low-molecular-weight heparin for presumed uteroplacental thrombosis and review in one week
options.rationale: Low-dose aspirin is used as prophylaxis for pre-eclampsia and FGR when commenced before 16 weeks gestation. Starting aspirin at 28 weeks provides no benefit for established placental insufficiency. There is no evidence to support empirical anticoagulation with LMWH in this setting. The priority is timely delivery rather than attempting to treat established placental disease. (Source: RANZCOG FGR guideline)

options.text: Admit for continuous cardiotocography monitoring and plan to continue the pregnancy until at least 34 weeks to optimise neonatal outcomes
options.rationale: While maximising gestation improves neonatal outcomes, attempting to reach 34 weeks in the setting of absent end-diastolic flow with brain-sparing at 28 weeks carries substantial risk of fetal death. The balance of risks favours delivery after corticosteroid administration. Continuous CTG alone is insufficient to prevent adverse outcomes when Doppler parameters indicate this degree of placental failure. (Source: ISUOG FGR guideline)

explanation.summary: Early-onset FGR (before 32 weeks) secondary to placental insufficiency is characterised by abnormal umbilical artery Doppler findings, progressing from raised pulsatility index to absent and then reversed end-diastolic flow. MCA brain-sparing indicates fetal redistribution of blood flow to vital organs. The ductus venosus Doppler provides additional information about cardiac function, and an abnormal a-wave is a late and ominous finding. Management requires balancing the risks of prematurity against the risks of continued exposure to placental insufficiency. At 28 weeks with absent end-diastolic flow and brain-sparing, delivery after corticosteroid administration is recommended.
key_points: Absent end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery with brain-sparing on MCA Doppler indicates significant placental insufficiency requiring delivery planning
Antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone 11.4 mg IM x 2 doses, 24 hours apart) should be administered before preterm delivery for fetal lung maturation
Constitutionally small fetuses have normal Doppler studies and do not require early delivery
explanation.pearls: In early-onset FGR before 32 weeks, absent end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery is an indication for antenatal corticosteroids and delivery planning within 48 hours - do not wait for ductus venosus abnormalities when multiple parameters confirm fetal compromise.

stem: A 33-year-old multigravida is seen at 35 weeks gestation for a routine growth scan. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated. She has no hypertension, proteinuria, or symptoms. The fetus is cephalic and structurally normal. A previous growth scan at 30 weeks showed the estimated fetal weight on the 25th centile. The current scan results are provided.

data_table.Ultrasound findings: Estimated fetal weight: 12th centile (decreased from 25th centile at 30 weeks); Abdominal circumference: 10th centile; Growth velocity (AC): Reduced - crossing centiles downward; Umbilical artery Doppler PI: Normal; Middle cerebral artery Doppler PI: Reduced (below 5th centile); Cerebroplacental ratio (CPR): Below 5th centile; Amniotic fluid: Normal deepest vertical pocket

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Reassure that all parameters are acceptable as the umbilical artery Doppler is normal and the EFW remains above the 10th centile, and continue standard antenatal care
options.rationale: Although the umbilical artery Doppler is normal and the EFW is above the 10th centile, this does not exclude late-onset FGR. The declining growth velocity crossing centiles and abnormal CPR below the 5th centile indicate placental insufficiency with fetal redistribution. In late-onset FGR, the umbilical artery Doppler often remains normal because the degree of placental disease is insufficient to raise umbilical artery resistance, making CPR the more sensitive marker. (Source: ISUOG FGR guideline)

options.text: Diagnose late-onset fetal growth restriction based on reduced growth velocity and abnormal CPR, increase surveillance, and plan delivery at 37 weeks gestation
options.rationale: This presentation is consistent with late-onset FGR. Although the EFW is above the 10th centile, the declining growth velocity with centile crossing and abnormal CPR (below 5th centile) indicate placental insufficiency. In late-onset FGR, the CPR is the key discriminator as the umbilical artery Doppler typically remains normal. ISUOG and RANZCOG guidelines recommend delivery at 37 weeks when there is reduced growth velocity combined with abnormal CPR, as continuing beyond this point increases the risk of stillbirth without meaningful neonatal benefit. Enhanced surveillance with twice-weekly CTG and weekly Doppler should continue until delivery. (Source: RANZCOG FGR guideline)

options.text: Administer antenatal corticosteroids and deliver immediately by caesarean section given the evidence of fetal brain-sparing on middle cerebral artery Doppler
options.rationale: Immediate delivery at 35 weeks is not warranted in this clinical scenario. While there is evidence of brain-sparing (low MCA PI and abnormal CPR), the umbilical artery Doppler is normal and amniotic fluid volume is preserved. Late-onset FGR follows a more indolent course than early-onset FGR, and the fetus tolerates this degree of redistribution. Delivery at 37 weeks balances the risk of ongoing placental insufficiency against the morbidity of late preterm birth. (Source: ISUOG FGR guideline)

options.text: Repeat the growth ultrasound in three weeks at 38 weeks gestation and plan routine delivery at 39 weeks if growth velocity normalises on the next scan
options.rationale: Waiting until 38-39 weeks for reassessment and delivery is too long in the setting of abnormal CPR with declining growth velocity. Studies including the TRUFFLE-2 trial indicate that late-onset FGR with abnormal CPR carries an increased risk of adverse perinatal outcomes if delivery is deferred beyond 37 weeks. The three-week interval also risks missing deterioration. Enhanced surveillance and delivery at 37 weeks is the appropriate strategy. (Source: RANZCOG FGR guideline)

options.text: Start low-dose aspirin 150 mg daily to improve placental perfusion and plan delivery at 39 weeks gestation if no further decline in growth velocity is observed
options.rationale: Low-dose aspirin initiated after the first trimester does not improve placental function in established FGR. Aspirin is a prophylactic intervention that must be commenced before 16 weeks gestation to have any effect on placental development. Starting it at 35 weeks provides no benefit and may falsely reassure the clinician. Delivery should be planned for 37 weeks based on the current findings. (Source: RANZCOG FGR guideline)

explanation.summary: Late-onset FGR (after 32 weeks) is more common than early-onset FGR but is more difficult to detect because the umbilical artery Doppler often remains normal. The cerebroplacental ratio (CPR) is the key discriminating tool, as it detects subtle redistribution of blood flow to the fetal brain that would be missed by assessing umbilical artery or MCA Doppler in isolation. Growth velocity assessment (change in centile over time) is also critical, as a fetus declining across centiles may have FGR even if the absolute EFW remains above the 10th centile. RANZCOG and ISUOG guidelines recommend delivery at 37 weeks for late-onset FGR with abnormal CPR, balancing stillbirth risk against neonatal morbidity of earlier delivery.
key_points: Late-onset FGR typically presents with normal umbilical artery Doppler - the CPR below the 5th centile is the key marker of fetal redistribution
Declining growth velocity with centile crossing indicates FGR even when the absolute EFW is above the 10th centile
Delivery at 37 weeks is recommended for late-onset FGR with abnormal CPR - earlier delivery increases neonatal morbidity without clear benefit
explanation.pearls: In late-onset FGR, the cerebroplacental ratio (CPR) below the 5th centile is a more sensitive marker of placental insufficiency than umbilical artery Doppler alone, and delivery is recommended at 37 weeks rather than 39 weeks when CPR is abnormal with declining growth velocity.

sources.label: Figueras F, Gratacos E. Ultrasound Obstet Gynecol 2014

stem: A 31-year-old woman at 33 weeks gestation presents with a 2-week history of progressive generalised pruritus that is worst on the palms and soles and disrupts her sleep. She has no rash, jaundice, or abdominal pain. Her blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg and urinalysis is normal. Investigation results are provided.

data_table.Blood results: Serum bile acids: 52 micromol/L (reference: <6 micromol/L); ALT: 78 U/L (reference: <35 U/L); AST: 65 U/L (reference: <35 U/L); Bilirubin: 18 micromol/L (reference: <20 micromol/L); Platelets: 245 x10^9/L (reference: 150-400 x10^9/L); INR: 1.0 (reference: 0.9-1.1)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Commence prednisolone 25 mg daily and plan delivery at 39 weeks gestation with weekly bile acid monitoring to assess treatment response
options.rationale: Prednisolone is not a recommended treatment for intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. It does not reduce bile acid levels or improve pruritus in this condition. Corticosteroids are used for other pregnancy conditions such as fetal lung maturation or autoimmune hepatitis, but not for ICP. (Source: RANZCOG ICP guideline)

options.text: Start colestyramine 4 g twice daily as first-line bile acid binding therapy and plan delivery at 39 weeks gestation with fortnightly bile acid monitoring
options.rationale: Colestyramine is a bile acid sequestrant that has been used historically for ICP-related pruritus but is poorly tolerated due to gastrointestinal side effects and can impair absorption of fat-soluble vitamins. It is not considered first-line therapy. Ursodeoxycholic acid is the preferred first-line agent. Additionally, delivery at 39 weeks would be too late for bile acids of 52 micromol/L, which fall in the 40-99 micromol/L range warranting delivery at 37 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG ICP guideline)

options.text: Commence ursodeoxycholic acid 250 mg twice daily with dose titration, weekly bile acid and liver function monitoring, and plan delivery at 37 weeks gestation
options.rationale: This is the correct management of intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy with bile acids in the 40-99 micromol/L range. Ursodeoxycholic acid is the first-line pharmacological treatment, started at 250 mg twice daily and titrated up to a maximum of 2 g/day based on response. Weekly monitoring of bile acids and liver function tests is recommended. RANZCOG guidelines recommend planned delivery at 37 weeks gestation when bile acids are between 40 and 99 micromol/L to reduce the risk of stillbirth while balancing neonatal morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG ICP guideline)

options.text: Start ursodeoxycholic acid 250 mg twice daily with dose titration, weekly bile acid and liver function monitoring, and plan delivery at 38 weeks gestation
options.rationale: While ursodeoxycholic acid is the correct first-line treatment, the timing of delivery at 38 weeks is not aligned with current RANZCOG recommendations for bile acid levels in the 40-99 micromol/L range. The recommended delivery timing is 37 weeks gestation for this category of ICP severity, as the risk of stillbirth increases after this point. (Source: RANZCOG ICP guideline)

options.text: Start rifampicin 150 mg twice daily as first-line therapy for severe pruritus, weekly bile acid and liver function monitoring, and plan delivery at 37 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Rifampicin is a second-line agent used for ICP pruritus refractory to ursodeoxycholic acid. It should not be used as first-line therapy due to potential hepatotoxicity and the need for careful liver function monitoring. First-line treatment remains ursodeoxycholic acid. Rifampicin may be considered if symptoms persist despite maximum dose ursodeoxycholic acid. (Source: RANZCOG ICP guideline)

explanation.summary: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP) classically presents with pruritus worst on the palms and soles, often in the third trimester, with no primary skin lesion. The diagnosis is confirmed by elevated serum bile acids (greater than 6 micromol/L). Ursodeoxycholic acid is the first-line treatment, improving pruritus and reducing bile acid levels. The timing of delivery depends on the peak bile acid level: 37 weeks for levels 40-99 micromol/L and earlier (34-36 weeks) for levels 100 micromol/L or above, reflecting the dose-dependent relationship between bile acid levels and stillbirth risk.
key_points: ICP presents with pruritus without primary rash, confirmed by elevated serum bile acids above 6 micromol/L
Ursodeoxycholic acid is first-line treatment, commenced at 250 mg twice daily and titrated to response (maximum 2 g/day)
Delivery timing is stratified by bile acid level: 37 weeks for 40-99 micromol/L and 34-36 weeks for 100 micromol/L or above
explanation.pearls: Ursodeoxycholic acid starting dose is 250 mg twice daily (max 2 g/day) for ICP, with planned delivery at 37 weeks when bile acids are 40-99 micromol/L.

sources.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 43: Obstetric Cholestasis

stem: A 28-year-old woman at 34 weeks gestation with a twin pregnancy presents with severe pruritus on her palms, soles, and trunk. She was commenced on ursodeoxycholic acid 500 mg twice daily one week ago after initial bile acids were reported at 65 micromol/L. She has no epigastric pain, visual disturbance, or headache. Her blood pressure is 122/74 mmHg. Repeat investigation results are provided.

data_table.Blood results: Serum bile acids: 112 micromol/L (reference: <6 micromol/L); ALT: 128 U/L (reference: <35 U/L); AST: 105 U/L (reference: <35 U/L); Bilirubin: 32 micromol/L (reference: <20 micromol/L); Platelets: 210 x10^9/L (reference: 150-400 x10^9/L); INR: 1.3 (reference: 0.9-1.1); LDH: 180 U/L (reference: 120-250 U/L); Blood film: No schistocytes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase ursodeoxycholic acid to 500 mg three times daily, add colestyramine 4 g twice daily, and plan delivery at 37 weeks with twice-weekly bile acid and liver function monitoring
options.rationale: With bile acids now above 100 micromol/L, delivery should not be deferred to 37 weeks. The PITCHES trial and RANZCOG guidelines indicate that bile acid levels above 100 micromol/L carry a significantly increased risk of stillbirth (up to 3.4%), and delivery between 34 and 36 weeks is recommended. Increasing ursodeoxycholic acid and adding colestyramine while waiting until 37 weeks exposes the fetuses to unacceptable risk. (Source: RANZCOG ICP guideline)

options.text: Administer vitamin K 10 mg orally, increase ursodeoxycholic acid to maximum dose, and continue monitoring with plan for delivery at 36 weeks based on serial bile acid levels
options.rationale: While vitamin K supplementation is appropriate given the raised INR suggesting fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption, the plan to deliver at 36 weeks does not reflect the urgency warranted by bile acids above 100 micromol/L in a twin pregnancy. Current guidelines recommend delivery between 34 and 36 weeks for severe ICP, and at 34 weeks in a twin pregnancy this is already achievable. The management should prioritise early delivery rather than continued monitoring to 36 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG ICP guideline)

options.text: Stop ursodeoxycholic acid as it has been ineffective, commence dexamethasone 12 mg daily for 3 days to reduce bile acids, and deliver at 37 weeks gestation after completing the course
options.rationale: Dexamethasone is not an effective treatment for reducing bile acids in ICP. While antenatal corticosteroids may be appropriate for fetal lung maturation before preterm delivery, they are not used to treat maternal cholestasis. Ursodeoxycholic acid should be continued even if bile acids are rising, as it may still provide partial benefit for pruritus and hepatoprotection. (Source: RANZCOG ICP guideline)

options.text: Administer vitamin K 10 mg orally to correct the coagulopathy, continue ursodeoxycholic acid at maximum tolerated dose, and plan delivery within the next 48 hours after fetal assessment
options.rationale: This is severe ICP with bile acids above 100 micromol/L, placing both fetuses at significantly increased risk of stillbirth. The raised INR of 1.3 indicates fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption from cholestasis, requiring oral vitamin K supplementation. RANZCOG guidelines recommend delivery between 34 and 36 weeks for bile acids above 100 micromol/L. At 34 weeks with a twin pregnancy and bile acids of 112 micromol/L, delivery within 48 hours after confirming fetal wellbeing and correcting coagulopathy is appropriate. Ursodeoxycholic acid should be continued until delivery. The normal platelet count, normal LDH, and absence of schistocytes help exclude HELLP syndrome. (Source: RANZCOG ICP guideline)

options.text: Admit for continuous cardiotocography of both twins, commence intravenous vitamin K 10 mg, and await bile acid levels to trend down on the current dose of ursodeoxycholic acid before deciding on delivery timing
options.rationale: While admission and cardiotocography are reasonable, awaiting bile acid levels to trend down is inappropriate at this severity. Bile acids of 112 micromol/L represent severe ICP with a high stillbirth risk that warrants expedited delivery rather than expectant management. Oral vitamin K is preferred over intravenous in this setting as there is no active bleeding or urgent surgical need. The coagulopathy can be corrected orally while planning delivery. (Source: RANZCOG ICP guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe ICP with bile acids above 100 micromol/L carries a stillbirth risk of approximately 3.4%, which is significantly higher than the risk at lower bile acid levels. The relationship between bile acid concentration and stillbirth risk is dose-dependent, with a steep increase above 100 micromol/L. Delivery between 34 and 36 weeks is recommended in this severe category. Coagulopathy from fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption (vitamins A, D, E, K) may develop and should be corrected with oral vitamin K before delivery. It is important to differentiate ICP from HELLP syndrome, which presents with hypertension, low platelets, haemolysis (schistocytes, elevated LDH), and elevated transaminases.
key_points: Bile acids above 100 micromol/L define severe ICP with significantly increased stillbirth risk warranting delivery at 34-36 weeks
Raised INR in ICP indicates fat-soluble vitamin K malabsorption and should be corrected with oral vitamin K before delivery
Normal platelets, normal LDH, and absence of schistocytes help differentiate severe ICP from HELLP syndrome
explanation.pearls: Oral vitamin K 10 mg should be administered to correct the coagulopathy in severe ICP (INR above 1.1), and delivery should occur between 34 and 36 weeks when bile acids exceed 100 micromol/L.

sources.label: Ovadia C et al. Lancet 2019 - PITCHES trial and bile acid thresholds
RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 43: Obstetric Cholestasis

stem:
A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with a sensation of vaginal heaviness and a bulge that she can feel at the vaginal introitus, worsening by the end of the day. She reports difficulty evacuating her bowels and occasionally needs to digitally support the posterior vaginal wall to defecate. She is otherwise well, has a BMI of 28 kg/m2, and had three vaginal deliveries.

She is not sexually active. On examination, there is a Stage II cystocele and rectocele with the leading edge reaching the hymen. She has not tried any treatment for this condition.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer for vaginal hysterectomy with anterior and posterior colporrhaphy as she has a symptomatic multi-compartment prolapse requiring definitive surgical correction
options.rationale: Surgical management is not the initial approach for a patient who has not yet tried conservative measures. Guidelines recommend a trial of conservative management before surgery. Surgery carries risks including mesh complications, recurrence, and anaesthetic risks, particularly in older patients. First-line treatment should include pelvic floor muscle training and a vaginal pessary trial. (Source: RANZCOG prolapse guideline)

options.text: Commence topical vaginal oestrogen and refer for sacrocolpopexy with mesh as this provides the most durable repair for multi-compartment prolapse in postmenopausal women
options.rationale: Sacrocolpopexy is a major abdominal procedure typically reserved for vault prolapse or recurrent prolapse, not as first-line management. While topical vaginal oestrogen is appropriate to improve tissue quality, surgery should not be the initial step when the patient has not attempted conservative management including pelvic floor muscle training and pessary use. (Source: Continence Foundation Australia)

options.text: Advise weight loss to a BMI below 25 kg/m2 and commence oral hormone replacement therapy to improve pelvic tissue support, with review in six months to assess symptom improvement
options.rationale: While weight management is a reasonable general recommendation, weight loss alone is unlikely to resolve Stage II prolapse. Oral HRT is not the preferred route for treating prolapse - topical vaginal oestrogen is preferred as it directly improves local tissue quality. This plan also omits the two key conservative interventions: supervised pelvic floor muscle training and vaginal pessary trial. (Source: Continence Foundation Australia)

options.text: Commence topical vaginal oestrogen and prescribe a bulk-forming laxative for bowel symptoms, with review in three months and surgical referral only if symptoms persist unchanged
options.rationale: While topical vaginal oestrogen and managing constipation are appropriate components of care, this plan omits the two key conservative interventions: supervised pelvic floor muscle training and a vaginal pessary trial. Pelvic floor muscle training has Level 1 evidence for improving prolapse symptoms, and a pessary can provide immediate symptom relief. These should be offered before considering surgery. (Source: RANZCOG prolapse guideline)

options.text: Commence topical vaginal oestrogen, refer for supervised pelvic floor muscle training, and offer a trial of a vaginal pessary with review in three to six months to assess symptom response
options.rationale: First-line management of symptomatic pelvic organ prolapse is conservative, consisting of supervised pelvic floor muscle training, vaginal pessary trial, and topical vaginal oestrogen in postmenopausal women. Pelvic floor muscle training has strong evidence for improving prolapse symptoms and should be supervised by a pelvic floor physiotherapist. A vaginal pessary (ring or Gellhorn) can provide immediate mechanical support and symptom relief. Topical vaginal oestrogen improves local tissue quality and pessary tolerance. Surgery is reserved for women who fail or decline conservative management. (Source: RANZCOG prolapse guideline)

explanation.summary: Pelvic organ prolapse is common in postmenopausal multiparous women. The POP-Q staging system classifies prolapse by the position of the leading edge relative to the hymen. Stage II prolapse reaches within 1 cm of the hymen. First-line management is conservative: supervised pelvic floor muscle training (minimum 3 months), vaginal pessary trial, lifestyle modifications (weight management, avoiding heavy lifting, managing constipation), and topical vaginal oestrogen for postmenopausal women. Surgical options are considered when conservative measures fail or are declined by the patient.
key_points: First-line management of symptomatic prolapse is conservative: pelvic floor muscle training, vaginal pessary, and topical vaginal oestrogen in postmenopausal women
Supervised pelvic floor muscle training by a specialist physiotherapist has Level 1 evidence for symptom improvement in Stage I-II prolapse
Surgery is reserved for patients who fail or decline conservative management after an adequate trial period of three to six months
explanation.pearls: Topical vaginal oestrogen (e.g., oestriol 0.5 mg pessary or cream nightly for 2 weeks then twice weekly) improves pessary tolerance and local tissue quality in postmenopausal women with prolapse.

sources.label: NICE NG123: Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse in women

stem:
A 34-year-old woman presents 6 months after the vaginal delivery of her third child. She reports involuntary urine leakage when she coughs, sneezes, or lifts her toddler. She denies urgency, frequency, nocturia, or pain. She does not leak during sleep. She has no urinary tract infection symptoms and a midstream urine culture was negative. She has a BMI of 26 kg/m2 and is otherwise well.

On examination, there is mild anterior vaginal wall descent but no prolapse beyond the hymen. A cough stress test in standing is positive with a small volume leak.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer for supervised pelvic floor muscle training with a continence physiotherapist for a minimum of three months with a structured exercise program and regular review
options.rationale: Supervised pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) is the first-line treatment for stress urinary incontinence. Level 1 evidence demonstrates that a supervised program of at least 3 months duration is superior to unsupervised exercises. The program should include both strength and endurance training of the pelvic floor muscles. The Continence Foundation of Australia and eTG both recommend this as initial management before considering further investigation or surgical options. (Source: Continence Foundation Australia)

options.text: Commence oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily for 3 months to reduce detrusor overactivity contributing to her urinary incontinence and review symptom response at follow-up
options.rationale: Oxybutynin is an antimuscarinic medication used for overactive bladder and urge urinary incontinence, not stress urinary incontinence. This patient has classic stress incontinence symptoms (leaking with coughing, sneezing, lifting) without urgency, frequency, or nocturia. Anticholinergic medications are ineffective for stress incontinence and would cause unnecessary side effects including dry mouth, constipation, and cognitive impairment. (Source: eTG)

options.text: Refer for urodynamic studies to confirm the diagnosis of stress urinary incontinence before commencing any treatment, as clinical assessment alone is insufficient in multiparous women
options.rationale: Urodynamic studies are not required before initiating first-line conservative treatment for clinically obvious stress urinary incontinence. The history (leaking with raised intra-abdominal pressure, no urgency symptoms) and positive cough stress test provide sufficient clinical evidence. Urodynamics are indicated before surgical intervention, when the diagnosis is uncertain, or when initial conservative treatment has failed. (Source: Continence Foundation Australia)

options.text: Refer for mid-urethral sling surgery as a definitive treatment given she has completed her family and has demonstrated stress incontinence on clinical examination with a positive cough test
options.rationale: Mid-urethral sling surgery is effective for stress incontinence but is not first-line management. Conservative treatment with supervised pelvic floor muscle training should be trialled for at least 3 months before considering surgery. Up to 70% of women with stress incontinence improve with PFMT, potentially avoiding the risks of surgery including mesh complications, voiding dysfunction, and de novo urgency. (Source: RANZCOG)

options.text: Recommend general fitness exercise including Pilates and yoga for core strengthening, reduce caffeine intake, and review in six months to assess whether symptoms have resolved spontaneously
options.rationale: While general lifestyle advice including caffeine reduction is reasonable, general core strengthening exercises such as Pilates and yoga are not equivalent to targeted supervised pelvic floor muscle training. Evidence supports specific pelvic floor muscle training with a continence physiotherapist as the effective intervention, not general fitness exercises. Some exercises like high-impact activities may worsen symptoms. A six-month wait-and-see approach without specific PFMT delays effective treatment. (Source: Continence Foundation Australia)

explanation.summary: Stress urinary incontinence is the involuntary leakage of urine with increased intra-abdominal pressure (coughing, sneezing, lifting, exercise) in the absence of detrusor contraction. It is common postpartum, particularly in multiparous women. First-line treatment is supervised pelvic floor muscle training with a specialist continence physiotherapist for at least 3 months. Urodynamic studies are not required for initial management when the clinical picture is clear. Surgery (mid-urethral sling) is reserved for women who fail conservative treatment.
key_points: Supervised pelvic floor muscle training for a minimum of 3 months is first-line treatment for stress urinary incontinence with Level 1 evidence
Antimuscarinic medications such as oxybutynin are for urge incontinence, not stress incontinence
Urodynamic studies are indicated before surgical intervention or when the clinical diagnosis is uncertain, not before initiating conservative treatment
explanation.pearls: Supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least 3 months with a continence physiotherapist improves stress urinary incontinence in up to 70% of women and should be trialled before any surgical intervention.

stem:
A 35-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with a 12-month history of progressively heavy menstrual bleeding. Her periods occur regularly every 28 days and last 8 to 9 days. She soaks through a super pad every 2 hours on her heaviest days and has passed clots. She reports fatigue and exertional dyspnoea. She has no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding.
